Tech Report: Science at the Frontier: How scientists use ChatGPT

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery.
  • Scientific progress depends on researchers asking latest questions and finding ways to answer them.
  • OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How more than 1,800 scientists used ChatGPT—and what they expect AI to mean for scientific discovery. Explore the findings in our fresh report.

Scientific progress depends on researchers asking latest questions and finding ways to answer them. AI is becoming part of that work, but we’re still learning where it helps and what it could mean for discovery.

OpenAI’s Economic Research team studied more than 580,000 scientific messages from 1,819 scientists in the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers summer pilot and surveyed 251 participants.

In a recent development, scientists used ChatGPT across the research process, from reviewing literature to analyzing evidence and developing ideas. Surveyed participants estimated that the same work, at the same quality, would have taken 1.9 times as long without AI. And 98% of those who answered our question about discovery timelines expected AI to accelerate discovery in their field.

By default, OpenAI does not use participants’ data from the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to train its models. To protect researchers’ privacy, we used tools called automated classifiers to sort messages by the type of research activity, such as reviewing literature, writing code, or analyzing data. The research team could see those categories, but did not read the underlying messages or ChatGPT’s responses.

We studied how scientists used ChatGPT across the research process.

For each scientist, we calculated the share of their scientific messages in each activity, then averaged those shares, giving every scientist equal weight. Percentages are rounded; other research activities accounted for less than 1%.

We looked at how scientists used ChatGPT for ideation. The figures below describe their messages about research ideas.

of the time, scientists brought a specific question for ChatGPT to work with.

of the time, scientists brought an idea and asked ChatGPT to refine it.

of the time, scientists asked ChatGPT to suggest a research question.

The message could not be categorized into one of the other activities.

We asked scientists across different fields to imagine a discovery that would take 10 years without AI and estimate how long it would take with AI.

250 respondents answered this question. Respondents could select multiple fields, so field groups overlap. Percentages are rounded and may not total 100%.

We measured how often scientists followed up to clarify, check, or revise ChatGPT’s responses across different research activities.

Average percentage of each scientist’s requests that led to a follow-up.

In a recent development, we asked scientists who expected faster discovery to explain why. Three reasons stood out in their answers.

Find more promising research questions.

Pursue a wider range of questions.

Industry observers note that scientists could give multiple reasons. Percentages show the share of all 367 reasons identified in 224 written responses.

Recent findings suggest that scientists in this study used ChatGPT to explore ideas, analyze evidence, write code, and communicate their findings. Their responses also point to ambitions beyond saving time: finding more promising questions and pursuing a wider range of research.

Recent findings suggest that understanding whether those expectations translate into faster discovery will take more research. Progress will also depend on the funding, staff, and experimental capacity scientists need to test their ideas.

We want to empower more scientists to explore what AI can make possible in their work. Alongside this research, we’re expanding ChatGPT for Academic Researchers⁠, with free access for more than 200,000 researchers around the world. Helping scientists turn their ideas into discoveries that improve lives is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

For more on this study, read the complete paper⁠(opens in a upcoming window) or download the key findings⁠(opens in a new window).

Recent findings suggest that “Tools like ChatGPT are helping us accelerate scientific discovery. It’s really a playground for a scientist like myself.”.

Strengthening the fight against online child sexual abuse with upcoming tools and support

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.
  • Industry observers note that today, we’re releasing a fresh tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators.
  • Industry observers note that it is well⁠(opens in a latest window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh tools, practical guidance, and partnerships will help prevent, detect and respond to online child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Industry observers note that today, we’re releasing a fresh tool to detect child sexual abuse material (CSAM), interventions that interrupt harmful behavior and point people toward help, practical resources for developers, and support for child-safety law enforcement investigators. These efforts build on our Child Safety Blueprint and our ongoing work to detect, block, and report abuse. For parents, the goal is simple: technology that helps keep children safe, with people in control.

Industry observers note that it is well⁠(opens in a latest window) established⁠(opens in a new window) that combatting online child predators requires coordination across many organizations. Individual companies like OpenAI have a responsibility to prevent our technology from being exploited by predators to harm children, and we also must work together with the broader industry, child safety organizations and law enforcement to advance our collective efforts to protect children online.

We’re building on our current protections with the release of a new image classifier that can detect potential CSAM, including AI-generated material. This new classifier looks for visual signs of abuse, helping teams identify novel images that may not have been seen before. It returns scores that help reviewers decide which images may need attention first. This is the first CSAM classifier with broad availability that has a specific signal on indicating if CSAM may be AI generated.

Our teams trained, evaluated, and designed the classifier for real-world deployment with assistance from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC)⁠(opens in a latest window), a nonprofit that operates the CyberTipline, a centralized reporting hub for the online exploitation of children.

We’re offering access to the classifier to vetted organizations through the OpenAI API at no cost, making CSAM detection more accessible to child safety organizations and the broader industry, including those with teams of varying sizes.

Sources indicate that child safety is an industry-wide matter that requires strong collaboration across organizations and a variety of solutions. We’ve engaged the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window) and ROOST⁠(opens in a new window) to help us share access to this new tool, and we are strong supporters of tools developed by others such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window) CSAM detection system. In addition, we recently began participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program⁠(opens in a new window), where we will share and receive signals relating to online child sexual exploitation and abuse to strengthen cross- platform collaboration.

We’ve tested the classifier internally and with early partners to measure how much abusive material it detects, how often it flags other images, and how it can support safety teams. Their feedback helped us identify weaknesses and improve the system.

Sources indicate that early tests suggest the classifier can help reviewers focus on abusive images while reducing review of false positives. In an evaluation of user-uploaded images, we compared the new classifier with our current protections and found:.

The latest classifier could reduce review work: we estimated that it would flag 48% fewer images while finding roughly the same number of abusive images as the existing tool.

Images flagged by the fresh classifier were about twice as likely to contain abuse.

Early access partners have also evaluated how the classifier supports their own safety teams. In fal⁠(opens in a upcoming window)’s testing on human-reviewed production images, reviewers confirmed 72% of the classifier’s high-confidence flags as novel CSAM. invideo AI⁠(opens in a new window)’s testing revealed one in four flagged cases led to a ban. In SafetyKit⁠(opens in a new window)’s evaluations involving drawings or animations that sexualize children, the classifier detected 90% of cases.

According to recent reports, more information about the classifier is available in the CSAM classifier model card⁠(opens in a latest window). Organizations interested in the classifier will be able to request access through our intake form⁠. We’ll continue improving the classifier with feedback from those that use it.

Industry observers note that we already prohibit CSAM, train our models to refuse requests for it, and take action against accounts that violate our policies. We’re building on those safeguards with new product warnings in ChatGPT that interrupt attempts to find abusive material, explain the consequences, and point people toward help to stop harmful behavior.

The warning makes clear that sexualizing children causes harm, including when the requested material is AI-generated. Alongside the warning, we’ll remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours, while keeping specialist support available to help people stop harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions and ultimately account closure or reports to authorities.

Recent findings suggest that we developed this approach with input from organizations and academic advisors that research and develop programs to prevent child sexual abuse, including Protect Children⁠(opens in a upcoming window), the Lucy Faithfull Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), Dr. Caoilte Ó Ciardha, Researcher & Honorary Reader in Forensic Psychology at the University of Kent and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial⁠(opens in a new window) of deterrent messages.

According to recent reports, the protection of children online doesn’t end with detection. We’ve published CSAM guidance⁠(opens in a fresh window) to give developers practical steps to prevent abuse, detect harmful content, and act on it. Developed with input from the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), NCMEC⁠(opens in a new window), and the Internet Watch Foundation⁠(opens in a new window), it is designed for organizations at different stages of building their safety systems.

Industry observers note that the guidance provides clear rules, ways for people to report concerns, detection tools, and processes for reviewing and reporting suspected abuse. It also explains how safety identifiers can help developers connect misuse to individual users and how to support the people reviewing sensitive content. Developers can use it alongside tools such as our newly introduced image classifier, Moderation API⁠(opens in a new window), ROOST’s self-hosted review console Coop⁠(opens in a new window), and dedicated CSAM detection services such as Thorn’s Safer⁠(opens in a new window).

Our commitment to collaboration and supporting the broader developer ecosystem also is reflected in our work with Anthropic and Google to jointly commission latest guidance on responding to disclosures of child sexual exploitation and abuse in AI systems. Recently published by the Tech Coalition⁠(opens in a new window), this guidance provides developers with practical recommendations for addressing these sensitive situations.

We’ve already seen this guidance lead to increased numbers of developers accessing child safety tooling and registering to report CSAM to NCMEC.

In a recent development, protecting children also means supporting the specialist child safety investigators working to find victims and stop abuse. As we’ve discussed publicly with Thorn⁠(opens in a new window), AI can help investigators organize and prioritize information and reduce unnecessary exposure to abusive material.

In a recent development, we’re also supporting child-safety law enforcement units with new tools and trainings on how to use AI in their investigations, including dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. At launch, the first tool will help investigators review lengthy chat logs and legal process returns, identify potential connections, and create timelines, with findings linked to source material.

The initial training is planned as an overview and demonstration, supported by a practical field guide that teams can refer to afterward. It will introduce the tools and how they fit into investigative work. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. Future iterations of the training will be proposed at regional, national and international conferences.

These efforts share one goal: preventing harm to children and strengthening the response when abuse occurs. We’ll continue improving our safeguards while empowering child protection organizations, developers, researchers, and investigators with the tools, resources, and expertise they need to protect children, combat exploitation, and bring perpetrators to justice. By working together, we can harness the power of AI to make a meaningful difference in the fight against child sexual exploitation and abuse.

Broadening access to AI for scientists

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.
  • According to recent reports, the program began as a pilot in July.
  • Sources indicate that participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 16, 2026 · Research · Science.

We’re expanding the ChatGPT for Academic Researchers program to give up to 200,000 researchers worldwide free access to ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, the program began as a pilot in July. Applications for the next round open Monday, November 23. We’ll award 50,000 upcoming grants to eligible researchers on a first-come, first-served basis. Each grant gives the recipient and up to two collaborators free access to ChatGPT Plus. If you’re already on the waitlist and qualify, we’ll email you before applications open with instructions for activating your account.

Sources indicate that participants can use OpenAI’s frontier models and get training on how to use ChatGPT in their research. By default, we don’t use data shared through the program to train our models.

Waitlist signups by country or territory as of November 12, 2026. Darker colors indicate more signups on a logarithmic scale.

20,000 researchers in 33 countries have joined the program since the pilot began in July. Shuqi Li, a researcher at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, looks for fresh drug targets that could ultimately shorten tuberculosis treatment. He is exploring whether ChatGPT can help link lab and patient data to speed up antibiotic development. Arthur Porto, assistant curator of AI biodiversity at the Florida Museum of Natural History, and his team uses AI tools to turn photographs of museum specimens into searchable databases. They also created a 3D model of a butterfly whose wings change color as you turn it, just like the real specimen.

It has been revealed that we’re also publishing Science at the Frontier: How Scientists Use ChatGPT, upcoming research from our Economic Research team examining how more than 1,800 researchers used ChatGPT during the program’s summer pilot. Surveyed participants estimated that, without AI, the same research work at the same quality would have taken nearly twice as long.

We want more researchers to have the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions and make discoveries that improve people’s lives. That is central to our mission of ensuring that AGI benefits all of humanity.

Industry observers note that the program’s summer pilot helped us understand how researchers use ChatGPT and how we can improve their experience. Based on feedback from researchers, we’re moving away from lottery-based selection. For the next round, we’ll provide access to the first 50,000 applications who meet the eligibility requirements.

According to recent reports, the pilot gave researchers access to ChatGPT Pro. When we reviewed pilot usage, we found that most participants would have stayed within ChatGPT Plus usage limits. Based on that finding, we’re offering Plus for upcoming grants so we can extend access to more research teams.

Each grant for this round covers the recipient and up to two collaborators, supporting up to 150,000 researchers. Our goal for the program as a whole is to reach 200,000 researchers, double the goal we announced when the pilot rolled out in July.

It has been revealed that we’ll continue learning from participants about the application process, the capabilities they need, and the support that helps them use these tools in their research. This feedback will help us refine the program and shape future rounds.

Different scientific fields will use AI in different ways, and researchers will need different kinds and levels of support. We’re working with scientific communities to understand those needs and shape our tools, training, and programs around them.

Our support also includes helping scientific communities turn AI-generated results into deeper understanding and fresh discoveries. In mathematics, we contributed $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative⁠ to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI.

We’re also providing different ways for researchers and institutions to access our tools. ChatGPT for Academic Researchers is just one way we’re helping researchers access advanced AI tools.

Through ChatGPT Edu⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), universities can give their campus communities access to ChatGPT for research, teaching, and learning, with tools for analyzing data and administrative controls for managing access.

According to recent reports, for researchers working in biology, GPT‑Rosalind⁠ brings together specialized biological reasoning and access to scientific tools and databases. The Rosalind Academic Strategy⁠ helps bring these capabilities to eligible labs at U.S. universities, offering up to 30 seats at no cost for up to 12 months. Access to GPT‑Rosalind requires approval through our trusted-access process.

Visit our researcher access guide to learn more about ChatGPT Edu, GPT‑Rosalind, and ChatGPT for Academic Researchers.

It has been revealed that as these efforts grow, researchers’ experiences will help us understand where our tools are useful, where they fall short, and what support is needed. We’ll use that feedback to improve our programs, develop training and learning resources, and create opportunities for researchers to exchange approaches with one another.

Our goal is to give more researchers the tools and support to pursue ambitious questions—and to keep improving that support as their research and our capabilities evolve.

Learn more about the program⁠(opens in a new window).

Introducing OpenAI for Chile

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we’re launching OpenAI for Chile, a partnership with the Government of Chile, led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, to support responsible AI adoption in public administration, build civil servants’ skills and help local startups develop useful AI applications.
  • The partnership builds on Chile’s National AI Policy and action proposal⁠(opens in a latest window), which support talent development, research and responsible adoption.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we’re launching OpenAI for Chile, a partnership with the Government of Chile, led by the Ministry of Science, Technology, Knowledge and Innovation, to support responsible AI adoption in public administration, build civil servants’ skills and help local startups develop useful AI applications.

The partnership builds on Chile’s National AI Policy and action proposal⁠(opens in a latest window), which support talent development, research and responsible adoption.

The Memorandum of Understanding was signed on the sidelines of Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World conference in California, with Minister Ximena Lincolao leading the agreement on behalf of Chile.

The partnership is supported by the U.S. Department of Commerce’s American SI Exports Program⁠(opens in a new window), of which OpenAI is an anchor partner, helping Chile advance its own AI ambitions through public sector innovation, skills development, and entrepreneurship.

The partnership will explore technology adoption in the ministry’s administrative processes, including potential support from OpenAI on adopting fresh models, alongside advice and training for ministry personnel.

Recent findings suggest that for civil servants, the partnership will explore practical AI literacy, upskilling and reskilling tailored to their roles. Activities could include workshops and a train-the-trainer approach, covering effective use of AI tools, checking outputs, protecting sensitive information and maintaining human oversight.

Sources indicate that to support Chile’s AI startup and innovation ecosystem, the partners will explore access to relevant OpenAI programs and technology, practical learning, technical guidance and mentorship. Cooperation could also connect entrepreneurs with public institutions, universities and other local partners to develop applications that support Chile’s economic development and public-service priorities.

A joint task force of ministry and OpenAI representatives is expected to agree priorities and an initial workplan, with leads, milestones and measures of success for each activity.

Specific activities, eligibility, resources and access to technology will be agreed separately. The MoU sets no investment or purchasing commitment. Activities will be subject to appropriate safeguards for privacy, information security and responsible use.

Recent findings suggest that openAI for Chile is part of OpenAI for Countries, our global initiative to help countries use AI to advance their national priorities, strengthen their economies and expand opportunity. We work with governments and local partners to turn AI’s potential into practical benefits for their people.

Astra for Law leads in legal intelligence

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that our latest model configuration earned leading marks on multiple benchmarks.
  • It has been revealed that today, we're releasing an updated Astra for Law that is state-of-the-art on Harvey LAB-AA and a top performer on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench.
  • According to recent reports, astra for Law is a model configuration of GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠, our latest, most powerful frontier model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that our latest model configuration earned leading marks on multiple benchmarks. Every ChatGPT Enterprise customer can now request access.

It has been revealed that today, we're releasing an updated Astra for Law that is state-of-the-art on Harvey LAB-AA and a top performer on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench. We are also enabling all ChatGPT Enterprise customers to request access through the Trusted Access Program, including through the API.

According to recent reports, astra for Law is a model configuration of GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠, our latest, most powerful frontier model. It pairs GPT‑6.2 Astra with an expanded legal search index and instructions for researching a question, weighing the authorities, and writing the answer. Today’s configuration earned full credit on the LAB-AA tests nearly 40% more often than did the runner-up, GPT‑6.2 Astra.

Since we introduced Astra for Law in September⁠ to a small group of firms, including Cooley⁠, Ropes & Gray⁠, and Sullivan & Cromwell⁠, our research team has made rapid innovations to improve its legal reasoning and expand its legal search index by over a third. On Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a latest window), the share of research answers that passed every check rose from about 46% to 53.8% in less than two months.

As the world grows more complex, lawyers occupy an increasingly crucial role. They shape nearly every system we rely on: they negotiate the agreements that move commerce, defend people’s rights in courts, and draft the laws we all live by. That’s why we’ve made law a research priority at OpenAI: to put the best intelligence in the hands of the best lawyers.

Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) tests whether a model can take a legal assignment from start to finish. LAB-AA⁠(opens in a new window) is Artificial Analysis’s version of that test. It tests the models on 120 assignments developed by Harvey across 24 areas of law – everything from drafting deposition outlines to reviewing commercial leases to strategizing ownership changes in acquisitions. To earn full credit, an answer must meet every requirement of an assignment without hallucinating, i.e., making a material claim that is not supported by the source documents.

Astra for Law ranked first, earning full credit on 20.8% of assignments, ahead of GPT‑6.2 Astra at 15.0% and Muse Wonder Full at 13.1%.

Astra for Law ranked first at 20.8%, earning full credit about 59% more often than Muse Wonder Full, the highest-scoring non-OpenAI model.

In a recent development, astra for Law also earned that top score with 54% less output per assignment than the highest-scoring non-OpenAI model in the evaluation, averaging about 64,000 output tokens per assignment, compared with 139,000 for Muse Wonder Full. For legal teams paying by usage, this can mean the difference between staying within budget and blowing through it.

According to recent reports, each dot is a model configuration. Higher means more assignments earned full credit; farther left means fewer output tokens, which include the text a model generates as it reasons and writes. Astra for Law averaged about 64,000 output tokens per assignment and earned full credit on 20.8%, compared with 139,000 and 13.1% for Muse Wonder Full. No configuration shown matched Astra for Law’s score using fewer output tokens.

Industry observers note that hallucinations are unacceptable in legal work. A single invented citation can cost a lawyer a client’s trust, credibility in court, and a reputation built over years. That’s why reducing hallucinations has been a priority for Astra for Law. In Artificial Analysis’s latest LAB-AA comparison, Astra for Law tied (with GPT‑6) for the lowest rate of material hallucinations: 0.03 per assignment, compared with 0.59 for Claude Opus 5.5 (the next lowest non-OpenAI model). Notably, Astra for Law's performance on this eval included zero material hallucinations for tasks that met the all-pass criteria.

Recent findings suggest that astra for Law averaged 0.03 material and 0.06 minor hallucinations per assignment. Claude Opus 5.5 averaged 0.59 material and 0.51 minor hallucinations per assignment, about 20 times as many material hallucinations and 8.5 times as many minor ones.

Across the same 120 assignments, Artificial Analysis counted hallucinated claims that could mislead a reader on a substantive point. Astra for Law averaged 0.03 such errors per assignment, tied for the lowest rate in the comparison and roughly half the rate for regular GPT‑6.2 Astra (0.06).

Industry observers note that every OpenAI configuration tested had fewer hallucinations than Claude Opus 5.5, the best non-OpenAI result on this measure. Opus 5.5 averaged 0.59 material hallucinations per assignment, about 20 times as many as Astra for Law.

We've made law a research priority at OpenAI, dedicating a team of researchers to accelerate innovation for frontier legal intelligence. One early measure of their progress comes from Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench⁠(opens in a new window), where practicing lawyers set questions about U.S. federal and state law. An answer has to cover every required point and pass the source checks. In September, Astra for Law earned full credit on about 46% of questions. In Vals AI’s November 16 evaluation, it earned full credit on 112 of 208 questions (53.8%), a gain of about eight percentage points in under two months. Across all questions, it earned 90.9% of the available points, including partial credit.

In less than two months, the share of legal research questions on which Astra for Law earned full credit rose from about 46% to 53.8%, a gain of about eight percentage points.

Astra for Law (green) sits in the small cluster of top performers on Vals AI’s Legal Research Bench.

Building Astra for Law as a model configuration lets us stay on the bleeding edge of the frontier, in this case GPT‑6.2 Astra⁠. On top of this foundation, we iteratively refine Astra for Law’s specific settings and instructions in response to practitioner feedback, teaching it how to reason and write like a seasoned lawyer. We also continuously hone its tools, such as the legal search index. Since September, we’ve grown the index by 34%, adding over 80 million new URLs, including across international jurisdictions such as the UK, Australia, and Canada. Today, the updated index spans over 310 million URLs and covers more than 99.9% of published U.S. precedential case law⁠(opens in a new window).

It has been revealed that the chart below highlights how the model configuration takes advantage of both the speed of frontier innovation and builds on top of that the specific requirements that make it powerful for lawyers. On Harvey’s own Legal Agent Benchmark, GPT‑6 Astra met every requirement on 4.6% of assignments. GPT‑6.2 Astra tripled performance, completing 14.6% under the same conditions. With the legal configuration, that rose to 16.2%, completing 11% more questions than GPT‑6.2 Astra.

This chart shows both the rate of development in frontier intelligence, as well as the impact of the model configuration. The full-credit rate more than tripled from GPT‑6 Astra to GPT‑6.2 Astra, then rose another 11% with the legal configuration. This test comes from Harvey’s own LAB (separate from the previously discussed LAB-AA).

The most interesting possibilities for Astra for Law are being shaped by the lawyers who are using it for their day-to-day work. Across law firm customers and OpenAI’s own legal team, early customers are building references around their practice, inviting tougher challenges to their arguments, and finding new ways to respond to changing legislation.

For example, early users at OpenAI are using Astra for Law to:.

Give your argument its strongest opponent. A common use for Astra for Law is as a sparring partner. A competition lawyer gives it a reading of a statute and asks it to argue the other side, drawing on legislative history, court decisions, and versions of the law in other languages.

Find the line between a recommendation and a requirement. A policy lawyer looking at a proposed oversight bill wanted to know how much power an independent reviewer would have. If the reviewer called for a fix, would the developer have to make it? For questions like these, the lawyer puts a plain-English account of each obligation beside the bill’s exact words, so she can make fast judgment calls about which reading the text supports.

Start the first call with outside counsel on the hardest question. When the business is considering entering an unfamiliar industry, a product lawyer uses Astra for Law to map which rules would apply to the proposed activity. Instead of spending the first call asking for high-level advice, the lawyer can bring outside counsel what’s actually at glitch.

It has been revealed that turn a stack of policies into a workflow. A legal program manager used Astra for Law to turn regulatory procedures and manufacturer policy into a workflow for colleagues handling incoming cases, enabling them to automate when to ask for more information, when to close the case, and when to escalate it to a lawyer.

Build the guide you wish came with the statute. A competition lawyer paired Astra for Law with ChatGPT’s site-building tools to annotate legislation the team uses regularly. A colleague reading a provision can hover over a term for its definition, follow a link to the materials that explain it, and see what the team advised the last time that provision came up.

According to recent reports, starting today, every ChatGPT Enterprise customer can request Astra for Law through the Trusted Access Program in the admin console. If your team already has access, select gpt-6.2-astra-law in ChatGPT. Customers can also request API access to build Astra for Law into their own tools using this form⁠.

The legal profession is at an inflection point. As technology changes what businesses can do and the world becomes increasingly complex and interconnected, lawyers have an unprecedented opportunity to shape how we make sense of the moment, not just for the businesses they advise but for all of us who live by the rules they help write.

We believe the best lawyers, equipped with the best intelligence, can meet that moment. We’re only at the beginning. We can’t wait to see where you take the profession.

Introducing ChatGPT for Sales

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Help every seller shorten the sales cycle, from finding the right accounts to following through on customer commitments, with a new Sales experience and over 30 new and expanded partner plugins.
  • Sources indicate that we’re introducing ChatGPT for Sales to help every sales team understand customers better, spend less time on busywork, and close more deals.
  • In a recent development, the new Sales plugin from OpenAI gives you ready-to-use workflows for everyday sales work, from deciding which accounts to pursue to preparing for a call and drafting the follow-up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Help every seller shorten the sales cycle, from finding the right accounts to following through on customer commitments, with a new Sales experience and over 30 new and expanded partner plugins.

Sources indicate that we’re introducing ChatGPT for Sales to help every sales team understand customers better, spend less time on busywork, and close more deals. It includes our new Sales plugin with dedicated skills for sellers, and more than 30 new and enhanced partner plugins in ChatGPT, so you can use information from the tools your team already relies on to prepare for calls, tailor proposals, and follow up faster.

In a recent development, the new Sales plugin from OpenAI gives you ready-to-use workflows for everyday sales work, from deciding which accounts to pursue to preparing for a call and drafting the follow-up. Sales teams work best when everyone has a shared understanding of the customer. Which accounts are worth pursuing? What does a buyer need to move forward? Which deals need attention, and why? The answers often sit across teammates, prospecting tools, customer calls, and the CRM. Bringing that information together gives teams more time to make informed decisions and follow through on customer commitments. That starts with the work you do every day.

ChatGPT for Sales brings your tools, customer context, and sales workflows into one place. It also gives your team access to partner plugins, so ChatGPT can use customer context from your existing tools to help move opportunities forward. Choose the partner plugins that fit your sales process.

Recent findings suggest that create content and equip sellers. Learn your sales process and the latest product updates with Confluence, Guru, and Seismic. Rehearse pitches and practice handling objections with ChatGPT Voice. Build tailored presentations with ChatGPT Slides, Gamma, Figma, or Canva, or create an interactive demo or ROI calculator with ChatGPT Sites.

Industry observers note that manage accounts and advance deals. Bring together account context from Salesforce, HubSpot, Close CRM, or monday CRM to prepare for calls, review customer commitments, and plan next steps.

According to recent reports, find and engage buyers. Combine account signals from Apollo, Clay, and Common Room with ChatGPT’s web research to understand what’s changing at an account and identify reasons to reach out. Use Outreach or Salesloft to proposal your outreach.

It has been revealed that turn customer conversations into action. Use call notes from the Meetings plugin in ChatGPT, Gong, Otter.ai, or Granola to understand buyer priorities, capture agreed next steps, and draft follow-ups.

It has been revealed that track performance and spot deal risk. Use signals from Backstory to identify deals that need attention. Analyze connected sales data with the Data plugin in ChatGPT or Hex to explain what changed in the pipeline and where to focus next.

Prepare quotes and agreements. Bring in Docusign, Ironclad, PandaDoc, or ServiceNow CPQ to help prepare quotes and agreements when a buyer is ready to move forward.

It has been revealed that you can also keep work moving between conversations by delegating to your dot—an always-on agent in ChatGPT. Your dot can use these same plugins and customer context to prepare meeting briefs, track deal updates, and proactively bring you relevant changes and proposed next steps for review.

Industry observers note that use ChatGPT to build a prioritized account list from your CRM information and prospect research from tools like ZoomInfo and Clay. Ask why each account fits, identify missing information, and refine the list around your team’s priorities. Then turn that research into outreach with a specific reason to engage—all in the same conversation.

Recent findings suggest that before a meeting, ask for a briefing that brings together account history, previous calls, and the buyer’s priorities. Explore what still needs an answer, then turn that preparation into a customer-specific pitch with Gamma or Canva. Refine the story in the conversation before your meeting.

After a call, have ChatGPT draft the follow-up, capture agreed next steps, and prepare updates to the customer record. Refine the message in the conversation and review the proposed changes. With connected tools like Attio, you can save the next step to your CRM from ChatGPT.

Ask ChatGPT to help you understand what is holding up a deal, using CRM history and customer conversations. With Rox, you can also ask a dot to check the deal each morning, flag changes that need attention, and prepare a meeting brief or follow-up sequence for your review.

See a few examples from across the sales ecosystem showing how these tools work in ChatGPT:.

From account research to deal follow-through, hear how sales teams are putting ChatGPT for Sales to work.

Industry observers note that install the Sales plugin⁠(opens in a upcoming window) to get started, and learn more about ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugins. Availability of partner plugins and features varies by plan, region, and workspace settings.

Sources indicate that chatGPT Business and Enterprise admins can enable ChatGPT for Sales for your team by opening the Admin Console⁠(opens in a new window), selecting your workspace, and selecting Plugins. Make the Sales plugin and relevant partner plugins available for members to install, or install them⁠(opens in a new window) by default for your team. Review access to the required apps and the actions they can use. Workspace members can complete any required account connections when prompted.

Recent findings suggest that we’re continuing to build ChatGPT for Sales and the partner plugin ecosystem around the work sales teams do every day. Our goal is to bring more of that work into ChatGPT, with connected tools and customer context that carries from finding an opportunity to preparing for a conversation and following through.

Strengthening NATO and allied cyber defenses with AI

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Governments and national cyber agencies protect the systems that people, public services and economies depend on.
  • OpenAI works with NATO’s Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) to provide NATO’s core institutions with access to advanced cybersecurity models, helping protect Allied networks.
  • In a recent development, NATO’s early use of OpenAI tools highlights how capable cyber defenders can put frontier models to work, supporting NATO’s mission of safeguarding the freedom and security of its member states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Governments and national cyber agencies protect the systems that people, public services and economies depend on. Through Daybreak, we’re putting advanced AI into the hands of trusted defenders for authorized security work, from reviewing software and investigating suspicious activity to validating vulnerabilities, and developing and testing fixes.

OpenAI works with NATO’s Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) to provide NATO’s core institutions with access to advanced cybersecurity models, helping protect Allied networks. NATO has used up to 300 billion raw input and output tokens per month as part of this work.

In a recent development, NATO’s early use of OpenAI tools highlights how capable cyber defenders can put frontier models to work, supporting NATO’s mission of safeguarding the freedom and security of its member states. It also helps strengthen cyber expertise across multinational teams responsible for protecting Allied networks around the clock, and creates lessons that can benefit defenders across Europe and the broader Alliance.

According to recent reports, openAI also supported⁠(opens in a upcoming window) the 2026 Crossed Swords exercise. Organized by the NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCOE), the exercise included a new training stream in which participants built, deployed, and evaluated AI agents for cyber operations, using OpenAI Daybreak in the technical environment. The training put participants alongside AI agents as operators, with an emphasis on maintaining human oversight.

OpenAI remains fully committed to NATO’s principles for responsible AI adoption and to delivering solutions that are safe and secure.

Beyond NATO, we have already provided access to our cyber models to defenders in Europe, including the EU’s ENISA and national cyber agencies in France (ANSSI), Germany and Poland.

Industry observers note that the Ministry of Digital Transformation of Ukraine is using⁠ OpenAI’s Daybreak tool to strengthen the cyber defence of civilian infrastructure. The initiative is designed to help Ukrainian teams identify software vulnerabilities and develop and test fixes more quickly, supporting defenders who protect essential services amid persistent cyber attacks.

Recent findings suggest that the EU’s cyber agency, ENISA, used our models to identify four vulnerabilities in software used across EU institutions, with fixes published for all four (1⁠(opens in a latest window), ⁠(opens in a new window)2⁠(opens in a new window), ⁠(opens in a new window)3⁠(opens in a new window), ⁠(opens in a new window)4⁠(opens in a new window)). A November ⁠(opens in a new window)joint report from ENISA and CERT-EU⁠(opens in a new window) also describes a review of 27 software projects using frontier models including OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak, and tools including the Codex security plug-in. Across the models tested, 95% of the 88 potential complications assessed by software maintainers were confirmed as genuine, demonstrating the value of combining AI with human expertise.

It has been revealed that CERT Polska used OpenAI models to help identify six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS⁠(opens in a latest window) and coordinated their disclosure with the vendor. Researchers directed the work, tested findings on real systems and verified their impact, with AI accelerating analysis and the exploration of potential vulnerabilities. MikroTik released fixes, which CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it had observed, giving network operators a concrete way to protect affected devices.

We will continue working with governments, national cyber agencies and international partners to turn frontier AI capability into stronger, safer, more resilient systems, helping defenders find weaknesses, fix them faster and protect the services people rely on every day.

#18647. Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2309 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work.
  • Industry observers note that GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work.
  • On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. Both models deliver better results on demanding tasks with fewer output tokens, so you can get more done within your usage limits. For businesses and developers, that means frontier performance at costs that make sense at scale.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work. Its slides, spreadsheets, and documents read less like AI, and more closely follow the templates you provide and the conventions of your field. It writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design.

On Agents’ Last Exam, which tests multistep professional work, GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a new high, scoring 5.2 points higher than GPT‑6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost.

Agents’ Last Exam evaluates models on long-horizon professional workflows. Its leaderboard results for Fable 5.2 exclude nine tasks that used a fallback model.

We believe GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. It sets a upcoming high on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1, which tests how well models can carry out scientific work in a terminal. GPT-6.2 Astra scores 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than one-third the cost. It also sets a new high on the Vals Science Index, which asks models to interpret real biological data and run experiments to infer how a simulated system works.

In the API, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT‑6 Astra’s, with a 60% discount on cached input ($8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens). GPT‑6.2 Sol keeps GPT‑6.1 Sol’s API token prices. On several benchmarks, both models come close to or outperform other leading models at a small fraction of the cost per task.

Compared with GPT‑6.1 Sol, GPT‑6.2 Sol is smarter, more efficient, and lets you complete more tasks on the same paid strategy. It powers through multistep agentic workflows, writes clearly and naturally, and is intuitive to collaborate with. Many employees at OpenAI use it as their default model for both technical and non-technical tasks.

In Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0, GPT‑6.2 Sol comes within 0.5 points of GPT‑6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost (both at max).

FrontierCode 2.0 evaluates whether changes to real codebases meet maintainers’ standards for merging.

Sources indicate that its speed and intelligence also make it ideal for the notable tasks people turn to AI for outside of work. On our recently released LifeVal⁠ evaluation, which measures performance on challenging everyday tasks, GPT‑6.2 Sol outscores GPT‑6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost.

LifeVal tests how well models handle everyday tasks tailored to someone’s needs, such as shortlisting kindergartens after a move, finding a home that fits a family’s budget and commute, or planning meals for a parent adjusting to a new diagnosis.

Industry observers note that we trained GPT‑6.2 Astra to create clearer, better-designed slides, spreadsheets, and documents that more closely follow the conventions professionals use in fields like law, sales, finance, and accounting. The writing is more direct and specific, with fewer generic takeaways and less filler.

Sources indicate that harvey LAB‑AA v1.1 uses legal assignments to test whether models can find the relevant facts across source documents, apply them to a detailed brief, and produce an accurate deliverable that meets every requirement. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a upcoming state of the art, more than doubling Claude Fable 5.2’s pass rate at about one-sixth the cost. Astra for Law⁠, our configuration of GPT-6.2 Astra for lawyers, scores even higher on this benchmark.

Harvey LAB‑AA tests legal work such as reviewing contract provisions. Its headline score gives credit only when a deliverable meets every grading criterion and contains no material hallucinations.

According to recent reports, our internal GDPval v2 benchmark is our next iteration of GDPval⁠ that measures complex, long-horizon workflows from real projects in sectors like consulting, finance, and design. GPT‑6.2 Astra leads the models we tested, up 6.2 percentage points from GPT‑6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens. GPT‑6.2 Sol improves 5.3 points from GPT‑6.1 Sol.

GDPval v2 consists of long-horizon knowledge-work assignments from real projects in sectors like finance, data science, biotechnology, and marketing.

According to recent reports, building a valuation workbook or writing an investment memo starts with finding the relevant figures in source files and working out how they fit together. Artificial Analysis’s AA‑AnalystAgent tests that work on real spreadsheets and reports. In one task, models use California Medicaid’s expenditure reports to calculate how much the program spent on medical transport. GPT‑6.2 Astra sets a upcoming high, answering 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts.

In a recent development, GPT‑6.2 Astra is our best model yet at designing slides and following slide templates, whether given an original file or even a screenshot. It can match the layout, colors, and typography down to the exact font size, and carry the template’s writing style into latest slides. Early testers found the decks easier to use directly with fewer edits, thanks to titles that state the main takeaway and concise body copy that focuses on the details readers need.

It has been revealed that we evaluated GPT-6.2 Astra on turning dense information into readable briefs and infographics for both technical and non-technical audiences. Examples included trading briefs and diagrams of agentic workflows.

In a recent development, GPT-6.2 Astra's documents were a significant step up from GPT-6 Astra. The writing and charts made it much easier to pick out the key points of a briefing, and the diagrams clarified complex systems by showing how the parts work together.

It has been revealed that in our Agent evals, GPT-6.2 Astra used 62% fewer tokens than GPT-6.1 Sol on complex legal-agent tasks. Astra was strongest on legal research, scoring higher than alternative models on 8 of the 10 research tasks we tested, across tax, M&A and litigation work.

It has been revealed that GPT-6.2 Astra is a notable step up from GPT-6 Astra, completing more than 3x as many Legal Agent Benchmark tasks in our evaluations with 34.5% fewer output tokens. For internal memos drafting tasks, GPT-6.2 Astra caught more weaknesses in the client’s position, and drafted filings made fewer unwarranted concessions.

Industry observers note that on the apps, dashboards and slides ClickUp Brain builds inside the workspace, GPT-6.2 Astra edged out our production model in blind testing. What stood out was how it got there: about 40% fewer tokens and 30% fewer review rounds.

It has been revealed that GPT‑6.2 Astra’s more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. Engineers can use that additional detail to check how components fit, see where loads shift as a design moves, and test revisions before building a prototype.

Sources indicate that we asked GPT‑6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road. Astra created the 3D model and wrote a Python solver to simulate complex dynamics between the tires and suspension, then animated the results in Blender. This enables engineers to quickly test latest designs and improve simulation accuracy over time.

GPT‑6.2 Astra can model a mechanical system part by part, giving engineers a way to show how it goes together and test how design changes affect its behavior.

Industry observers note that our team used GPT‑6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago’s Marina City towers into a lamp. The video follows the design from reference photos through CAD revisions to a physical lamp assembled by hand. The site, generated by GPT-6.2 Astra, can be used to create your own paper lamp.

GPT‑6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look and building elements around the actual goal of the site.

Those gains in visual reasoning and computer use carry over to 3D design. GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol can turn a written brief into an interactive browser experience, from a pinball table you can play to a recreation of the Colosseum you can explore from different angles. On Artificial Analysis’s AA‑3D, human judges try two blinded experiences built from the same prompt and vote for the one they prefer. GPT‑6.2 Astra ranks first with 1,318 Elo, followed by Claude Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and GPT‑6.2 Sol at 1,259.

According to recent reports, GPT-6.2 Astra is a huge leap forward for creative work. It makes Higgsfield Miracle possible, powering real-time video editing with pixel-level precision and giving creators ultimate creative control. In our internal 3D generation evals, it achieved the target result in one shot in 73% of cases, while GPT-6 Astra needed three or more iterations. This saves our creative team a lot of time and allows for more efficient fully agentic workflows.

GPT‑6.2 Astra has better judgment about how to execute a task, including matching its tools and effort to the workflow, and knowing when to use plugins versus computer use.

On coding, GPT-6.2 Astra is better at implementing and testing complex changes in existing codebases. Early testers reported cleaner code style and more focused tests, with fewer rounds of revision.

GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol mark another significant jump in cyber capabilities. They find and exploit vulnerabilities more effectively, write more secure code, and produce better patches, with substantial token-efficiency gains on several evaluations. Like GPT‑6 Astra⁠, 6.2 Astra and Sol meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework⁠.

It has been revealed that due to their increased capabilities, we’re launching GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol with tighter safeguards for higher-risk cybersecurity assistance. These protections reduce misuse risk, but also restrict some legitimate vulnerability research and security testing workflows. Through OpenAI Daybreak⁠, defenders can right now access GPT‑6 Sol with reduced cyber refusals on Daybreak Blue, in addition to our alpha for GPT-6 Astra, and GPT‑6 Cyber⁠ for advanced, authorized security testing on Daybreak Red. We will work to bring GPT‑6.2 models to Daybreak.

Recent findings suggest that we highlight key benchmark results below, using internal testing configurations with cybersecurity safeguards and classifiers disabled. See the accompanying system card⁠(opens in a fresh window) for full results and methodology.

Industry observers note that developers increasingly rely on coding agents to write production software, even as more capable agents lower the barrier to finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. PHP2Shell⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) highlighted how AI can help researchers uncover critical flaws. With GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol, we made defensive capabilities a core focus, introducing new training signals to help developers prevent and repair those flaws—writing secure code from the start and producing patches that preserve intended behavior.

We're deploying GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol with our strongest safeguards to date. We've tightened restrictions and strengthened the systems we use to monitor models⁠ and intervene when needed⁠.

According to recent reports, like GPT-6 Astra, in addition to meeting the Critical threshold for cybersecurity, both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet the High threshold for biological and chemical capabilities under our Preparedness Framework⁠. We’ve implemented protections to mitigate the associated risks, alongside increased restrictions across a set of potential dual-use biological and cybersecurity requests.

More details about our safeguards and testing are available in the GPT-6.2 system card⁠(opens in a fresh window).

GPT-6.2 Astra is our first externally released model to meet the High threshold for AI Self-improvement, which measures a model’s ability to accelerate AI research. A ‘High’ designation reflects our assessment that the model’s impact is equivalent to giving every OpenAI researcher an additional, highly capable research engineer as an assistant, relative to their 2024 baseline. We track this capability because models that can help develop future AI systems could also introduce new risks to safety, like accelerating progress faster than safeguards or human oversight can adapt.

To address these risks, we’ve built more oversight and controls into how we train and deploy our models. Before expanding internal access to GPT-6.2 Astra, we evaluated its alignment and verified that required safeguards were in place at each stage. We strengthened containment in our research environments⁠, and tested those protections with our most capable models. We also built Control Room⁠, a system that tracks research workloads and can halt further model output when intervention is needed. Our expanded monitoring⁠ examines models’ reasoning and actions across internal workloads and supported external deployments. It can automatically flag unauthorized behavior, and, where supported, pause workloads or conversations.

It has been revealed that both models performed similarly to GPT-6 Astra on most alignment evaluations, and took fewer improper actions in simulated workplace tasks. However, in two tests, they were more likely to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work, such as a missing file or unavailable search tool. We added instructions in Codex that substantially reduce these omissions, and we’re continuing to investigate the behavior.

GPT‑6.2 Astra costs significantly less per task than GPT‑6 Astra, driven by better token efficiency, a 20% discount on input and output tokens, and a deeper 60% discount on cached input tokens. Standard API rates per million tokens are $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output. GPT‑6.2 Sol carries forward GPT‑6.1 Sol’s rates of $2 for input, $0.10 for cached input, and $10 for output per million tokens.

For GPT-6.2 Astra & Sol, in order to improve cache reuse, help lower costs and latency, and preserve reasoning across turns, we recommend keeping prompt prefixes unchanged and appending newly introduced instructions⁠(opens in a new window) to the conversation.

Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 results for Fable 5.2 are as reported by Artificial Analysis⁠(opens in a new window) in the mini-swe-agent harness. Anthropic reported Fable 5.2's score of 74.6% at max reasoning in Claude Code.

#18637. Latest Update: Advancing chip design with OpenAI models

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1150 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Advancing chip design with OpenAI models

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, openAI’s models are swiftly improving the chips that power AI.
  • To measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings.
  • We started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, openAI’s models are swiftly improving the chips that power AI. In August,⁠ we shared how OpenAI engineers used our frontier models to accelerate the development of our first custom inference chip, Jalapeño. Here, we look more closely at the expert-level design improvements behind the Jalapeño gains and how we’re applying the same approach to deliver significant gains on third-party hardware with AMD.

To measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings. And to ground capability development in trusted evaluators, we’re working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation (EDA) tools that engineers already use to design and verify chips.

We started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. Even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements, such as:.

Industry observers note that in the vector unit, which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored both alternative logic implementations and how to divide computations across pipeline stages, finding opportunities to share hardware and reduce intermediate storage.

It has been revealed that in the matrix unit, an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Further improvements to dot-product logic and pipeline organization contributed additional savings across the block.

Recent findings suggest that across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates that model proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up⁠.

Industry observers note that we have partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and seen up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP. Our model identified further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits (SystemVerilog RTL). This represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months–unprecedented results at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for use in future versions.

We’ve observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect. The model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. It used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area.

AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by our model. Looking ahead, we expect further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline.

Our results on Jalapeño and AMD’s chips show that models can make improvements in production designs. To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, we tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores. PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs. OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip. Each is a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads.

Sources indicate that we gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput (the number of instructions the core can execute per second). For example, a change might let a core finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles but make each cycle take longer. Measuring throughput captures both effects.

We checked each design’s outputs in simulation. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area. For designs that passed, we measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models. We took the geometric mean across those workloads and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. That gave us an estimate of instructions per second. For each core, we assigned the best throughput we observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0. The charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero.

With a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores. GPT‑6.1 Sol also outscored GPT‑5.6 Sol on both.

Recent findings suggest that on the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT‑6.2 Astra has the highest mean score at the larger comparable budgets. Around 112,000 tokens, its score is about twice GPT‑6 Astra’s.

On the existing Ibex core, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches. GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol are closer together.

For the second task, we gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system. The model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, we kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task.

Sources indicate that at about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design. That held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT‑6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT‑6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets.

Recent findings suggest that on Ibex, GPT‑6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification. Its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets.

Starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions. Those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. Requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design.

We have demonstrated that our models can explore latest processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next generation flagship GPU and CPU. To ground model development in trusted evaluators and broaden the design challenges addressed, we’re partnering with Synopsys to train GPT‑Synopsys⁠(opens in a new window), a new model, to use Synopsys electronic design automation (EDA) tools the way expert chip designers do.
