#18577. How to simplify cloud access with Unified Access Policies, now in preview

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1199 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

How to simplify cloud access with Unified Access Policies, now in preview

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1199 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As organizations scale their cloud footprint to thousands of autonomous agents and microservices, you can accidentally create an operational bottleneck with strict Identity and Access Management (IAM).
  • Sources indicate that enter Unified Access Policies (UAPs), Google Cloud's next-generation access control engine in Cloud IAM, now in preview at no additional cost.
  • It has been revealed that this approach allows you to author a policy once and bind it across your organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

As organizations scale their cloud footprint to thousands of autonomous agents and microservices, you can accidentally create an operational bottleneck with strict Identity and Access Management (IAM). Meanwhile, administrators still need to enforce least privilege across thousands of resources without slowing down engineering velocity.

Sources indicate that enter Unified Access Policies (UAPs), Google Cloud's next-generation access control engine in Cloud IAM, now in preview at no additional cost. UAP consolidates allow and deny rules into one unified schema, and decouples policy definition from resource enforcement.

It has been revealed that this approach allows you to author a policy once and bind it across your organization. UAP governs human, workload, and first-class agent identities with your existing IAM policies. With UAP, you can radically simplify your access policies and manage them more easily at scale.

Traditional access policy models can push teams into a tough trade-off between Zero Trust access and pipeline speed due to three compounding forces:.

Fragmented schemas and permission sprawl: In granting thousands of granular permissions across cloud resources, administrators are forced to choose between either over-granting permissions from coarse roles with broad access, or wrangling two different syntaxes (APIs and mental models across allow and deny) just to define one workload's custom access posture.

According to recent reports, policies treated as snowflakes: Because legacy policies attach directly to individual resources, applying a standard developer or security baseline across 25 projects means duplicating and maintaining 50 separate allow and deny policy configurations in Terraform. This approach can create severe configuration fatigue and operational burden, with greater risk of misconfiguration.

Industry observers note that scale ceilings and explosion of agent identities: Modern cloud environments span human teams, federated workloads, service accounts, and autonomous agents that should never share generic service account credentials. As non-human and agent identities multiply, large enterprises routinely hit the hard 64 KB single-policy size limit on allow policies — requiring policy refactoring to onboard new teams or agents.

Helping platform and security teams address these access limitations demands a latest approach: an agent-ready engine on a unified control plane, designed to simplify, centralize, and scale access control.

According to recent reports, UAP removes cognitive burden for platform and IAM administrators, security architects, and agent administrators while shrinking your Infrastructure as Code footprint. UAP re-architects how policies are authored, bound, and enforced across your resource hierarchy because it’s built around a simpler authorization model.

1. Unified allow and deny syntax: Consolidate positive access grants and firm security guardrails into a single, auditable policy instead of reconciling separate allow and deny files.

It has been revealed that 2. Multi-binding support: A standalone policy binding acts as the connective tissue between your policy definition and target Cloud Resource Manager (CRM) nodes (organization, folder, and project). You can now bind a single UAP policy across up to 25 CRM targets in preview, eliminating duplicate Terraform blocks.

It has been revealed that 3. Expanded scale limits (5x effective policy size): UAP breaks through the legacy single-policy size ceiling by letting you attach up to five UAP policies (64 KB and up to 100 rules each) to any single CRM resource — scaling to 2,500 unique principals and 500 groups per resource.

Industry observers note that 4. Clear separation of concerns: Central security architects can author vetted baseline and guardrail policies at the organization node and delegate self-service binding to folder and project administrators, without letting local teams alter central rule logic.

5. Expressive permission wildcards and immutable guardrails: Replace brittle permission lists with prefix, suffix, and substring wildcards alongside predefined roles and action exclusions (excluded permissions).

6. Built-in readiness for agents: UAP treats agents as first-class principals (principal://agents.global...) rather than generic service accounts. Agent administrators can scope least-privilege allow and deny rules directly to individual agents or entire agent pools, combine UAP with short-lived, downscoped tokens, and build on an extensible foundation for human-in-the-loop and delegated agent authorization.

It has been revealed that 7. Day 1 parity across all four surfaces: At runtime, Cloud IAM evaluates your existing allow policies, deny policies and UAP policies concurrently across your resource hierarchy. Whether your teams prefer interactive workflows or declarative automation, UAP introduces with full create, read, update, and delete parity across the Google Cloud console, gCloud CLI, Terraform, and the Cloud IAM v3 REST API.

You can deploy your first policy to bring these powerful capabilities into your environment in just a few minutes.

While you can automate UAP through Terraform, gCloud CLI or REST API, you can also author and bind policies interactively in the Google Cloud console.

Step 1: Open the Unified Access Policies tabIn the Google Cloud console, select your target organization, folder, or project in the resource picker and navigate to IAM & Admin > IAM.

Alongside the existing Principals tab, select the newly introduced Unified Access Policies tab to view all policies in your scope — including their binding status, governed principals and rule types — and click + Create policy.

Unified Access Policies page lists all the policies managed at/ enforced at the scope picked by the customer (Project, Folder or Org).

Step 2: Define policy details and access rulesIn the Policy Details pane, enter a policy name and description, then build your access posture under Add rules:.

Select principals and exceptions: Choose a principal set or individual identity (such as dev group or agent identity) via + Add principal, and optionally exempt breakglass administrator groups via + Add exception principal.

Choose the rule effect and permissions: Select Allow (using predefined roles, individual permissions or permission wildcards) or Deny (using explicit permissions or wildcards, such as compute.googleapis.com/firewalls.*).

Combine rules in one policy: Click Add another rule to pair positive grants and deny guardrails in the same policy, while inspecting the live JSON configuration preview on the right.

Create Allow and/or Deny rules within a single UAP policy resource.

Step 3: Bind the policy and manage lifecycleProceed to the Enforcement step, select the target organization, folder, or project scopes where you want the policy to take effect, and click Bind policy.

Once created, you can click any policy on the Unified Access Policies landing page to open its Policy details view — where you can audit active rules and resource bindings, click View JSON to export the policy for IaC pipelines, or edit bindings as your environment evolves.

Every policy can be bound to a target resource through a binding. Leveraging separate bindings, a single policy can be enforced on multiple resources, unlocking simpler management at scale.

With your first policy securely enforced and managed, your security and platform teams can spend less time wrangling permission sprawl and more time driving business velocity.

With Unified Access Policies, we are excited to help you build a more secure, agile and future-ready cloud architecture that scales alongside your human and AI workloads.

To streamline your organization’s access management, explore the Unified Access Policies documentation, and try it in a test project — create and bind your first reusable UAP policy using gcloud CLI, REST API, or Terraform.

#18576. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task.
  • Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing.
  • Industry observers note that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each newly introduced agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

Industry observers note that while the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

Industry observers note that that is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

It has been revealed that funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:.

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with upcoming runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

It has been revealed that from there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the fresh one.

In a recent development, with funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and highlights exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three crucial properties:.

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:.

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

According to recent reports, before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

According to recent reports, when an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:.

It has been revealed that or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:.

Sources indicate that funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent states so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

According to recent reports, claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

This matters in a few different scopes:.

According to recent reports, published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

In a recent development, A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

In a recent development, the lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious.

According to recent reports, your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

In a recent development, full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hebbia sees gains in financial research in tests of GPT‑6 Astra.

Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested in Hebbia’s tests.

Percent of cited excerpts relevant to the question in Hebbia’s tests.

Percent of applicable presentation requirements met in Hebbia’s tests.

Percentage-point lead over the best alternative tested on presentation requirements.

According to recent reports, before a banker can recommend an acquisition to their client, they need to make sense of financial statements, customer contracts and management presentations. Hebbia’s Matrix helps bring that research together, linking answers to the documents behind them.

Hebbia tested OpenAI’s GPT‑6 Astra to improve two parts of that work: finding the sources a question requires and building a presentation that follows the banker’s brief.

It could work like this: a banker is helping their client assess a strategic acquisition of an industrial-software organization, with roughly 2,000 files to review. What makes its revenue durable? How does it compare with peers? In Hebbia’s hypothetical example, the banker could load the data room into Matrix and examine customer concentration, contract terms and churn in cited cells. Matrix could bring in peer filings and industry news to help develop the deal thesis, then turn that research into a diligence summary and valuation deck in the firm’s template.

In that workflow, GPT‑6 Astra selects documents or Matrix cells to support an answer, then turns the analysis into native PowerPoint slides that follow the user’s structure and guidelines.

“Traceability is really important to our customers because they’re basing millions of dollars of decisions on what the AI actually comes back with,” Kavita states. “Citations help with traceability as well as giving users confidence that the AI found the right answer.”.

In Hebbia’s tests, GPT‑6 Astra combined broader source coverage with highly relevant citations. It scored 13.6 percentage points above the best alternative tested on citing the required types of sources, while 99.5% of the excerpts it cited were relevant to the question.

Industry observers note that hebbia tested a prerelease build in August-September 2026, using the same financial research cases and grading criteria for each model. Domain experts wrote or audited the criteria against source documents.

“When you’re looking at a data room with thousands of documents, that’s extremely vital. Even a single percentage-point gain can yield a lot of marginal benefit,” Kavita says.

A presentation also has to look like work the banker would send to a client.

“I don’t want to create a deck and send that to my partner that looks like AI made it,” Kavita says. “I want it to be made in my firm’s branding, and I want it to look like a human-made slide.”.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6 Astra led on both following the brief and presentation quality. In Hebbia’s tests, it met 97.9% of the applicable presentation requirements, putting it 14.4 percentage points ahead of the best alternative tested on that measure. Other models traded off polish and adherence to the brief; GPT‑6 Astra ranked first on both.

“In the past, we’ve seen models that really shine on one or the other of these dimensions where they’re really good at craft, but the instruction following and adhering to guidelines is not strong, or vice versa. GPT‑6 Astra is the first model we’ve seen where it’s number one on both of those fronts,” Kavita says.

Industry observers note that in Hebbia, people can open a citation to see the underlying document and highlighted passage; slide footnotes lead back to the source material, too. A review could be as specific as checking a customer-concentration figure against the source table and correcting the reporting period before the deck goes to the investment committee.

Hebbia wants bankers to spend less time reformatting decks and checking sources, and more time assessing a deal. Kavita describes what a better first draft could make possible:.

Kavita sees a future role for agents that monitor information in the background and surface signals for finance professionals to assess.

“Imagine getting an key signal a few hours before your competitors,” she states. “You can get started thinking about it and see and process more opportunities that a human is not manually hunting. It can unlock a lot of value for our users.”.

Hebbia wants to build on these results to help finance professionals assess deals with research they can trace back to its sources.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Industry observers note that structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

In a recent development, note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

Recent findings suggest that IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:.

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

Introducing ambient networking for GKE

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption  and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment.
  • The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services.
  • The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

According to recent reports, network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption  and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment. Today, we are announcing the general availability of ambient networking for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). This milestone marks an key evolution in how your run service mesh on GKE, bringing a sidecar-less architecture into production. Introduced earlier this year, ambient networking decouples functionality traditionally provided as a service mesh from application workloads, allowing platform operators and developers to help secure, observe, and route traffic without the resource overhead and operational complexity of managing sidecar proxies.

The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services.

The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster.

At the same time, several Node-level management components operate securely within the gke-managed-ambient namespace:.

Ambient networking runtime interface (NRI) plugin: Integrates with the NRI to perform low-level network redirection, intercepting traffic to and from ambient-enabled application pods.

xDS agent (ambient agent): Runs inside the node proxy pod to receive xDS configuration updates from Traffic Director and request certificates from the GKE control plane on-demand.

Node proxy (L4 Envoy proxy): A high-performance, shared per-node Envoy instance that processes intercepted L4 traffic, enforces mutual TLS (mTLS), evaluates authorization policies, performs load balancing, and emits rich telemetry metrics.

Service pods: The user’s application/service pods communicate through the GKE node proxy to perform service to service mTLS across the cluster.

Together, these features combine to deliver a number of advanced capabilities for GKE environments:.

Recent findings suggest that zero Trust architecture: Ambient networking allows customers to establish a Zero Trust security posture. Traffic between workloads can be automatically encrypted using mutual TLS (mTLS) with managed workload identities, helping protect and secure service-to-service communication across the cluster.

Ambient networking delivers tangible value for GKE operators:.

Recent findings suggest that simpler operations: Traditionally, service mesh products rely on injecting sidecar containers directly into every workload pod. Ambient networking removes this sidecar dependency by shifting networking features to shared node components. This fully managed solution simplifies deployment and streamlines day-to-day cluster operations.

Recent findings suggest that simplified lifecycle management: When proxy logic is decoupled from application containers, lifecycle management is simplified. Upgrading proxy versions or applying configuration updates helps avoid restarting application workloads or scheduling downtime windows, enabling continuous availability for your services. Ambient networking can reduce administrative overhead and application disruption an average of four times annually by eliminating pod restarts required by CVE patches for L4 mesh usage.This fully managed solution can be installed either at cluster creation time or added to an existing cluster. Ongoing maintenance to the cluster components is handled by automated systems and is performed along with normal GKE cluster maintenance.

Simplifying adoption by removing the cost and complexity barriers of sidecars. Try it out in your GKE environment and experience the benefits of ambient networking:.

fully managed installation and upgrades.

service-to-service mTLS and authorization policies.

lower resource usage than sidecars.

See our documentation for more information: https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ambient-overview.

Pricing: https://cloud.google.com/products/gke-service-networking/pricing.

📅 03 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1564 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders.
  • We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach.
  • NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

According to recent reports, many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

It has been revealed that modernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

According to recent reports, neoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:.

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Industry observers note that multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

According to recent reports, pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

It has been revealed that to get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:.

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

Industry observers note that viDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

In a recent development, † Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:.

It has been revealed that we tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

People can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

It has been revealed that before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding upcoming documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

It has been revealed that so we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

Recent findings suggest that neoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:.

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

It has been revealed that neoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

Industry observers note that neoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Firm for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

#18568. Combatting adversarial distillation

Combatting adversarial distillation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2137 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.
  • Sources indicate that as frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly crucial role in how they can be used responsibly.
  • We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How we’re addressing safety risks of distillation and lessons we’ve learned for strengthening safeguards across the industry.

Sources indicate that as frontier AI models become more capable, safeguards play an increasingly crucial role in how they can be used responsibly. Adversarial distillation creates a path for bad actors to reproduce these capabilities without appropriate safeguards. An actor may use a frontier model’s outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities, then deploy it without comparable protections. For instance, an adversary might distill a model’s cyber capabilities and use the resulting model to help carry out cyberattacks that the original model would have refused to assist with or that its safeguards would have blocked.

We’re sharing how OpenAI detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, how we’ve strengthened protections for our models’ protected reasoning, and what we’ve learned that can help strengthen defenses across the industry.

Our approach to adversarial distillation combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities. These updated safeguards align more closely with those we use for biology and cybersecurity.

It has been revealed that we place particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting our models’ protected reasoning: the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. These traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model.

It has been revealed that we’ve strengthened our defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier prompt. The average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

Distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another. For example, a model can learn from another model’s answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. Beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks. Through adversarial distillation, a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them.

The concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology. A model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them; a model that assists with biological research could also help someone develop a harmful pathogen. If such capabilities were transferred to a model with weaker safeguards, it may provide assistance that the original model would have refused, or that the original safeguards would have blocked.

Our models help users with coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. A second model trained on many of those benign outputs may learn skills that also apply to offensive cybersecurity tasks. To better understand this, we study how distillation, especially involving reasoning traces, may transfer risky cyber capabilities.

In a recent development, in this setting, the model that produces the training data is called the teacher, and the model that learns from it is called the student. In an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, we used the content normally visible to owners—final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions—as our baseline for distillation, and tested how much additional cyber capability transfers when the student has access to the teacher’s exact reasoning traces.

Industry observers note that we started each training run from the same pretrained student model. We created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks. Each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. We evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments.

After supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. After reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets.1.

Sources indicate that our cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under our usage policies. Across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. We will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes.

Industry observers note that we defend against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of our safeguard stack. At the request level, model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls limit reasoning trace extraction. At the campaign level, we look for patterns in request-level and account-level signals that can reveal coordinated extraction attempts. In turn, attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing our safeguards.

Our defenses against adversarial distillation combine safeguards for individual requests with campaign detection and enforcement. Findings from investigations and automated red-teaming help strengthen those safeguards.

Industry observers note that adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. Adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners.

It has been revealed that we use input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning, and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments. These safeguards apply to both streaming and non-streaming responses.

In a recent development, tool-call coverage is crucial because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool’s arguments without including it in its final answer. Output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

It has been revealed that API-level protections restrict how protected reasoning can be reused across interactions and models. Our September disclosure described attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. We strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user’s encrypted reasoning.

With GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol, we tie a model’s protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. As new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning. If an earlier message is rewritten, our API drops the reasoning that followed it⁠(opens in a new window). We also prevent older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT‑6.2 Astra and Sol’s protected reasoning.

Recent findings suggest that when our systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract our models’ reasoning, we investigate the accounts responsible. When we identify violations, we enforce against the network of accounts, consistent with our policies and terms of service. Through investigations of each campaign, we generate insights that allow us to upgrade our defenses in order to better detect similar activity. We also share indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services.

It has been revealed that this work extends beyond our own platform. Our consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering our models. We work closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments.

Sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

It has been revealed that to measure how well our request-level safeguards work together, we test whether attackers can still extract protected reasoning in a setup that closely mirrors production deployments of our models and safeguards. In static evaluations, we replay a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning. In adaptive evaluations, automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds, which can uncover weaknesses the static tests miss.

According to recent reports, we also vary what testers can see. Black-box testing gives them the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. In our adaptive black-box evaluation, we tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. On GPT‑6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type. Both rates were substantially lower than on GPT‑6 Astra with its original safeguards. We’re now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT‑6 Astra as well.

GPT‑6 Astra defender with original safeguards.

GPT‑6.2 Astra defender with updated safeguards.

Extracting protected reasoning from an earlier request.

Extracting protected reasoning from the current request.

Industry observers note that attack success rate (ASR) in adaptive black-box red-teaming against GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Astra, aggregated across six attacker models. Lower ASR is better.

Industry observers note that we have seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on our platform this year, and shared initial findings in our September report. Our weekly enforcement actions against these campaigns have ranged in scale from thousands to tens of thousands of accounts, with the rate increasing significantly this past summer.

In order to measure the effectiveness of our efforts, we also track the prevalence of distillation abuse, as well as the time between detection and enforcement. Our objective is to constrain the volume and value of the data distillers are able to obtain, to increase the cost of distillation campaigns, and to shorten the time needed to respond to upcoming attacks. We continue to improve these defenses through adversarial testing and investigations.

Recent findings suggest that adversarial distillation also poses a national security risk. A foreign actor that reproduces advanced capabilities from a U.S. model can deploy them without the protections its developer put in place. In February, we briefed⁠(opens in a upcoming window) Congress on activity indicating that DeepSeek was attempting to distill U.S. frontier models. In September, we reported disrupting a campaign to extract our models’ protected reasoning and attributed a core part of that activity to individuals associated with Moonshot AI, the developer of Kimi. We blueprint to share more soon about recent campaigns we’ve disrupted.

We support legislation that would give the U.S. government more tools to identify and sanction foreign actors that illicitly extract capabilities from American AI models. We’ve also told Congress we support the Chip Security Act, the AI OVERWATCH Act, and the MATCH Act. Stronger export controls can limit adversaries’ access to the hardware needed to train frontier models. Distillation defenses make it harder to acquire some of the same capabilities from models already trained. Both efforts help maintain a U.S. lead in frontier AI, giving developers more room to slow a release when they need time to test safeguards.

Supporting the safe proliferation of frontier capabilities is an crucial goal of our anti-distillation work. Our experience so far suggests several useful steps that other model developers and platforms can take:.

It has been revealed that protect private reasoning across the full interaction. Check assistant messages and tool-call arguments for leaks, and restrict how encrypted reasoning can be reused across conversations and models.

Keep successful extraction attack logs found through red-teaming, production monitoring, or responsible disclosure as regression tests. Where appropriate, and consistent with applicable privacy policies, use those examples to improve model training and classifiers. When evaluating updated defenses, replay the original attacks and test whether an adaptive red-teamer can still find a way through those defenses.

Combine request-level mitigations with campaign-level investigation and enforcement.

Coordinate safeguard requirements and enforcement with deployment partners, and share expertise with other AI model developers, to ensure a high floor of distillation safeguards across the industry.

According to recent reports, we have previously also shared findings through the Frontier Model Forum⁠(opens in a upcoming window) and appropriate government information-sharing channels to help other developers strengthen their defenses while keeping the details attackers could exploit private. We’ll continue working with researchers, developers, and partners to share what we learn about emerging attacks and effective defenses.

As we make frontier AI broadly available, our defenses against adversarial distillation aim to reduce the risk that its capabilities are reproduced without adequate safeguards, supporting our mission to ensure that artificial general intelligence is deployed safely and benefits all of humanity.

Recent findings suggest that related work from Anthropic⁠(opens in a new window) reported a similar advantage when training on full reasoning transcripts rather than summaries on SWE-bench Verified, a software engineering benchmark. Our result shows this advantage extends to frontier cybersecurity.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mid-sized financial services firms are struggling to keep up with larger rivals on AI, with 80% of their leaders saying they are falling behind, according to research from TXP, a digital transformation business focused on tech consulting, development and resourcing.
  • The study points to a squeeze between thin in-house expertise and expensive outside partnerships.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mid-sized financial services firms are struggling to keep up with larger rivals on AI, with 80% of their leaders saying they are falling behind, according to research from TXP, a digital transformation business focused on tech consulting, development and resourcing.

The study points to a squeeze between thin in-house expertise and expensive outside partnerships.

In a recent development, the report, titled ‘Partner Dependency: The Hidden Cost of AI Projects’, polled 200 executives shaping AI strategy at mid-market organisations, among them businesses in financial services and insurance. Its central finding is that weak internal know-how, combined with poor handover of knowledge during projects, is locking firms into long-term reliance on external providers.

Industry observers note that some 65% of mid-market FS leaders said inadequate knowledge sharing has left them relying on outside partners to run or extend their AI initiatives. A further 56% admitted their staff cannot properly judge whether systems built by partners are working as intended.

Looking ahead, 77% expect this reliance to leave their own teams unable to oversee AI independently, and 79% fear it raises the likelihood that faults in AI systems will slip past unnoticed or prove impossible to resolve internally before they grow into larger problems.

According to recent reports, financial pressure is another concern. Of those surveyed, 91% believe dependence on partners could push expenses higher over time, while 56% stated spending on implementation partners has exceeded the value AI has delivered so far.

Trust in suppliers also emerged as an issue. Two-thirds of respondents claimed some partners had overstated their AI capabilities, with firms soon discovering a lack of genuine expertise. In such cases, organisations can face delayed projects or the added expense of hiring a second provider to finish the job.

TXP operates as a digital transformation specialist, offering tech consulting, development and resourcing services.

TXP chief operations officer Tim Hurst noted, “Mid-sized financial services firms often have smaller budgets and fewer internal skills than large enterprises. To keep pace with complex, critical technologies such as AI, partnerships and external support are essential. But without effective knowledge transfer, partner support often becomes partner dependence once the initial delivery phase ends. Costs quickly rise as projects extend beyond implementation into ongoing management. The value of AI is eroded and errors become harder to spot and fix, introducing security and operational risk.”.

Hurst added, “AI shouldn’t be the sole domain of larger, well-funded FS firms, and partners play a key role in levelling the playing field by helping the mid-market realise the benefits of AI. Mid-sized businesses should look for partners with strong security and compliance credentials who can integrate AI with their existing systems. Knowledge transfer and a clear plan to reduce long-term dependency should be built into every relationship from the start. Partners must build systems that work, and leave clients able to innovate long after they’ve gone.”.

Organisations across the region want firmer oversight of their sensitive data, technology and infrastructure, alongside greater resilience and less exposure to strategic dependencies on outside providers.

To meet these demands, Saviynt is running its identity security tools on S3NS infrastructure that carries SecNumCloud qualification, with Thales handling operations as a sovereign trusted third party.

Only EU residents employed by S3NS operate and support the service, which sits on PREMI3NS in an environment kept apart from Saviynt’s worldwide commercial cloud. This separation keeps data, infrastructure and day-to-day operations under local control.

Saviynt provides AI-enabled, cloud-native identity security for organisations handling highly sensitive workloads. The upcoming EU service adds to its existing data residency and private cloud options.

Because the offering runs independently of Saviynt’s global commercial cloud, customers can keep essential identity security functions running while cutting their reliance on external infrastructure and services.

Saviynt vice president of product management Niraj Gopal said, “Saviynt does not believe in a one-size-fits-all approach to sovereignty. Our EU Sovereign Identity Security Cloud complements our data residency and private cloud offerings, extending our portfolio with a modern, cloud-native, AI-enabled SaaS identity security solution. It is designed to help government agencies, regulated enterprises, and critical infrastructure providers protect their critical assets and systems while meeting stringent regulatory and sovereignty requirements.”.

In a recent development, saviynt field CIO Simon Gooch added, “European organisations should not have to choose between sovereignty and innovation.” He added, “With this offering, we are extending our cloud-native identity security platform to organisations that require complete sovereignty over their identity environments. By combining local control with operational independence, we are helping European organisations protect critical access, strengthen resilience and modernise identity security without compromising their sovereignty requirements.”.

Latest Update: Rebuilding AUTOMATIC1111 with Gradio Workflow

📅 10 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui.
  • Recent findings suggest that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes.
  • Industry observers note that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in our last post, we built five small gr.Workflow graphs and hinted at what it would take to build something as complex as AUTOMATIC1111's stable-diffusion-webui. In this post we walk you through Workflow1111, where we have rebuilt most of AUTOMATIC1111's feature set as a single workflow canvas.

Recent findings suggest that workflow1111 is a graph of eleven media pipelines built using seventy-three nodes. It brings together SOTA models for text-to-image, hi-resolution fix, image-to-image, prompt-matrix grids, VLM interrogate, detection-to-inpaint masks, ControlNet-style annotators, background removal, PNG Info storing, and image-to-video.

Industry observers note that you can run any of these pipelines by signing in with your Hugging Face account or providing an access token. Once you sign in, the model calls use your own quota.

👉 Try Workflow1111, or duplicate the Space and start rewiring it for your own use case.

All the media pipelines are built from the same four operator kinds covered in our last post and the official guide. Each node on the canvas wraps one operator, and the operator's inputs and outputs become the ports you connect edges to. As a quick reference on our four operator kinds: fn is a Python function, model is a model called through InferenceClient, space is another Gradio Space, and dataset is a row from a Hub dataset.

Let's go through the pipelines one by one.

This is the core pipeline. It has the controls you'd expect from A1111's txt2img tab: negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, width and height, plus a model_id field for choosing the checkpoint. The prompt goes through a prompt-builder fn node first, which appends the selected style preset and cleans up the text, then into a model node that calls the checkpoint through Inference Providers. A post-process fn node writes the generation parameters into the PNG's metadata on the way out, which is what the PNG Info pipeline reads back later.

It has been revealed that in Automatic1111, hi-resolution fix first upscales the txt2img output and then runs a second denoising pass. Here it's a two-node detour instead. The text-to-image result goes into a FLUX.1-Kontext model node with a refine instruction ("enhance fine detail and micro-texture, keep the composition identical") and comes back sharper and larger.

In a recent development, that same Kontext node doubles as the image-to-image tab. Upload an image, describe the change you want, and it returns the edited image.

Start with a rough prompt like "A lighthouse in a storm." This pipeline sends it to a Qwen3-4B model node, and a small fn node turns the reply into a clean list of tags, capped at forty: "stormy sea, wet rocks, dramatic composition, low angle shot, volumetric lighting, ominous tone." You can connect any diffusion model node to this output to render the image.

Sources indicate that there's no custom node involved, unlike in ComfyUI. In a Gradio workflow the LLM and the diffusion model are both ordinary model operators on the same canvas.

This is like AUTOMATIC1111's Interrogate button, with a VLM doing the interrogating instead of CLIP. Qwen2.5-VL looks at a night-market photo and writes a prompt that could have produced it. A ViT classifier node reads the same image and returns labels: restaurant 51.9%, tobacco shop 15.6%, toyshop 9.1%.

Both nodes use the same image input, so gr.Workflow runs them in parallel and you get both answers in roughly the time it takes to run one.

AUTOMATIC1111 makes you paint an inpaint mask by hand. This pipeline generates one from a detector instead. DETR finds six objects in a street photo (three people, a dog, a bicycle, and a car), and from there the workflow splits into two branches: one draws the detected boxes on the original image, the other turns them into a mask you can feed into an inpaint pipeline downstream.

The drawing and the mask creation both happen locally with Pillow and NumPy. Only the detection call leaves the machine.

According to recent reports, this is like AUTOMATIC1111's prompt matrix. A base prompt, "a lone oak tree," gets combined with four suffixes (at sunrise, in a thunderstorm, under the Milky Way, in autumn fog) by a fn node, and each variant goes to its own text-to-image node. A final node stitches the four results into one contact sheet.

According to recent reports, gr.Workflow has no loop operator, so the four text-to-image nodes sit side by side on the canvas. Since they're at the same dependency depth they run in parallel, and all four images start generating at once.

This is like the Extras tab in Automatic1111. There are two upscaler nodes, and they take different routes. The first is a local Lanczos resample in an fn node, which needs no network call and finishes as fast as Pillow can resize. The second is AuraSR ×4, and it's the first space node on the canvas: it calls a Space on the Hub and treats the result like any other node output.

It has been revealed that background removal works the same way. BRIA RMBG-2.0 is another space node, so the whole model lives in its own Space and this canvas just calls it in.

Canny, line art, sketch, luma-depth, and posterize are the preprocessors you'd normally get from the ControlNet extension in Automatic1111. Here, each one is a fn node written in plain NumPy, with no model behind it. On a pre-loaded example photo of a building facade, each annotator takes about half a second on CPU.

Recent findings suggest that there are 36 operator nodes in the app, 32 are fn nodes, and 22 of those run entirely in-process without a network call. Roughly two-thirds of the canvas keeps working if you lose your connection. Since these are regular Python functions, you can also test them directly, with no canvas, server, or GPU involved.

AUTOMATIC1111 stores generation details in the PNG's parameters text chunk, and the PNG Info tab reads them back. Workflow1111 does the same. The post-process node on the text-to-image pipeline writes the metadata, and this pipeline reads it back out, including the prompt, negative prompt, steps, CFG, seed, image size, and model.

In a recent development, the image node that PNG Info reads from also feeds a Wan 2.2 I2V A14B node, which animates it; in the demo example a sleeping fox wakes up and starts moving. There's no second upload box because one reference node can feed as many downstream pipelines as you need, so a single upload gets its metadata read and gets animated on the same canvas.

So far every model call has gone to someone else's hardware, through Inference Providers or a Space. That's why you can build and run something like Workflow1111 without a GPU of your own.

In a recent development, A fn node is just Python, though, so it can equally load a model locally and run it on your own GPU. FastVideo/fastvideo-fasth3-preview is a gr.Workflow app that does exactly that. It runs FastH3, a four-step distillation of MiniMax-H3, and generates video with a soundtrack on ZeroGPU.

The whole app comes down to one bound function:.

ZeroGPU gives the function a GPU when it needs one, then releases it when the call is done. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know about any of that. It just calls the fn node.

This isn't specific to Spaces either. Point bind= to a function that loads a local checkpoint, run .launch() on your own machine, and the Workflow1111 canvas can drive your own GPU.

Every output node on the canvas becomes a REST endpoint, with no routes written by hand. Workflow1111 exposes nine of them: /image, /edited_image, /generated_prompt, /recovered_prompt, /detected_objects, /x_y_grid, /upscaled_local, /annotator_map, and /png_info.

The same endpoints are also MCP tools. Launch with mcp_server=True (guide) and every output node highlights up as a tool an AI assistant can call. Point Claude Code, Cursor, or any MCP client at the server URL:.

Now an agent can generate an image, read a prompt back out, or run detection as steps in a larger task, with no glue code. Each caller sends their own token in the X-HF-Token header, so the Space holds none of its own.

AUTOMATIC1111 gave us the feature list, but the tool Gradio Workflow really gets compared to is ComfyUI, since both are node graphs. For a lot of what people want to build and ship, gr.Workflow covers the same ground.

The result is a multi-model pipeline that people can open in a browser, sign into, use right away, and call from code.

Workflow1111 has 73 nodes, but it started with just this:.

According to recent reports, bind= turns your functions into nodes, edges= connects them, and .launch() opens the canvas in your browser so you can keep editing there. When it's ready, gradio deploy puts the whole thing on a Space. The gr.Workflow guide has the full details, including the JSON schema and every operator type.

In a recent development, if you'd rather start from something that already works, open Workflow1111, hit Duplicate, and pick one of the eleven pipelines to change: delete nodes, swap models, rewire the flow. If you'd rather start smaller, the previous post has five workflows you can get running in about a minute each.

Sources indicate that whatever you build, post it on X and tag @gradio. We'd be happy to amplify your workflows.

According to recent reports, really impressive breakdown the part that stands out most is how the graph structure gives you free parallelism (the prompt-matrix and interrogate examples) without any extra orchestration code. The mix of fn, model, and space node types on one canvas also makes the ComfyUI comparison land well: you get custom-node flexibility from plain Python, but zero-code REST/MCP endpoints for free. Curious how complex a canvas can get before performance or maintainability becomes a concern has anyone pushed past 73 nodes.

According to recent reports, analisis yang sangat mengesankan, bagian yang paling menonjol adalah bagaimana struktur graf memberikan paralelisme gratis (contoh prompt-matrix dan interrogate) tanpa kode orkestrasi tambahan. Perpaduan tipe node fn, model, dan space pada satu kanvas juga membuat perbandingan dengan ComfyUI tepat: Anda mendapatkan fleksibilitas node kustom dari Python biasa, tetapi endpoint REST/MCP tanpa kode secara gratis. Saya penasaran seberapa kompleks sebuah kanvas dapat dibuat sebelum kinerja atau pemeliharaan menjadi masalah, apakah ada yang pernah melampaui 73 node?

VisionX AI, a Singapore-based AI-native RegTech firm operating as a standalone firm within Alpha Ladder Group, has debuted AEGIS, an in-house Large Graph Model (LGM) designed to detect and investigate financial crime, along with TraceX, the first product to run on it.

It has been revealed that AEGIS takes a different approach from tools that assess payments one at a time. It uses a Graph Transformer architecture and was pretrained on graph data drawn from financial transactions, so it learns how wallets, accounts and entities link together and how money travels between them.

Sources indicate that visionX AI pairs this proprietary model with LLMs from established providers in a hybrid set-up. AEGIS supplies the network intelligence, while the LLMs manage conversational interaction, reasoning and AI-supported investigative work. The combination aims to help banks and investigators surface concealed relationships, unusual fund movements and the wider criminal groups operating behind single transactions.

Recent findings suggest that the launch comes as illicit finance grows more networked. In July 2026, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) cautioned that criminal groups take advantage of the cross-border reach of virtual assets to defraud victims, dodge sanctions and launder money. Its findings revealed that illicit funds pass through stablecoins, cross-chain bridges, decentralised exchanges and mixers, where they blend with legitimate activity and become more difficult to follow and freeze.

According to recent reports, traceX, an AI-driven platform for blockchain tracing and investigation, is being developed for financial crime investigators and law enforcement bodies. It is intended to follow funds across linked blockchain addresses, flag suspicious patterns that connect separate cases, and produce investigative leads backed by traceable evidence and human oversight.

According to recent reports, reverse tracing, MegaMap network analysis, pattern recognition and case association are on the roadmap. Investigators retain decision-making authority, using TraceX’s suggestions as guidance, and every decision is logged.

VisionX began life as an incubated project inside MetaComp, tackling compliance and financial crime risks where traditional finance meets digital assets. It has since grown into a combined financial crime and compliance platform that underpins compliance intelligence for MetaComp’s StableX Agentic Network, which debuted as the StableX Network in November 2025.

Its offering includes VisionX KYT, which pools blockchain risk data from several independent analytics providers covering 1 billion wallets across 25 chains, and Web2.5 TxM, which merges identity, behavioural and network signals to monitor transactions across both traditional and digital asset markets.

In a recent development, spinning VisionX AI out as an independent business allows it to sell to a wider pool of financial institutions, digital asset firms and public-sector bodies. The manufacturer prepares to apply its graph intelligence technology to financial crime detection, fraud and scam prevention, compliance risk management and investigations.

The AEGIS name, short for Attention-based Entity and Graph Intelligence System, references the shield of Zeus in Greek myth that was lent to Athena, reflecting the technology’s protective purpose.

VisionX AI executive chairwoman Tin Pei Ling, who is also co-president of Alpha Ladder Group and MetaComp, remarked, “Financial crime operates through networks of people, entities and financial activities. To fight it, we need AI that understands the relationships between transactions. AEGIS is built to see this network. It learns how money moves between accounts and wallets, so it can spot the patterns that link activity which looks unrelated. Our ambition is to build AI-native financial crime tools that help institutions stay ahead of emerging threats.”.

VisionX AI CEO Summer Yu noted, “Individual cases often look unrelated, even when the same criminal network sits behind them. TraceX brings AEGIS into practical blockchain investigations, so investigators can identify patterns, connect cases and uncover those networks. AI demonstrates investigators where to look next, and their judgement and the evidence still decide the case.”.
