What’s new in Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a latest set of demands.
  • In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation.
  • Industry observers note that today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

As organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a latest set of demands. Moving from human scale to agent scale changes both how data pipelines run and how they are built: Teams and AI agents now use Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and agentic troubleshooting to build, submit, and diagnose Apache Spark pipelines while preparing multimodal datasets, performing feature engineering, and acting on live business signals around the clock. Over the past year, customer use of Managed Service for Apache Spark in serverless deployments has nearly doubled, with millions of jobs running each month as enterprises build on Google’s Agentic Data Cloud.

In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation. Managed Service for Apache Spark runs on Google Cloud's borderless lakehouse, so Apache Spark and BigQuery can read and write the same tables with high performance. Through Knowledge Catalog, both engines share centralized governance, consistent policies, detailed lineage, and semantic discovery for AI agents.

Industry observers note that today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments. Engineered to power both modern enterprise data pipelines and fast-growing agentic workloads, Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 introduces:.

A latest 4.0 runtime with Apache Spark 4.2: Standardized on Apache Spark 4.2, Java 25, Python 3.13 with Pixi, and Apache Iceberg 1.12, it is now available for both serverless and managed clusters.

A redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console and agentic troubleshooting: Onboard rapidly with a upcoming Overview page featuring a samples gallery, Lakehouse public datasets, and one-click VS Code authoring in Cloud Shell, manage all serverless and cluster workloads from a unified Jobs view, and use an AI agent to automatically diagnose job failures.

Third-party IDE integration with the Data Agent Kit: Configure MCP servers, skills, and API access to build and run Apache Spark pipelines directly from VS Code, Claude Code, and Antigravity.

Faster startups and Lightning Engine acceleration: Run on default Gen4 infrastructure with faster startups at no additional cost, and accelerate workloads with Lightning Engine for up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative.

This new runtime packages Apache Spark 4.2 (including Spark Declarative Pipelines and Real-Time Mode), Java 25, Scala 2.13, Apache Iceberg 1.12, Delta Lake 4.4, and Python 3.13 with Pixi for faster dependency management.

Managed Spark serverless and cluster workloads now run on the same modern stack whether written by a data engineer or generated by data engineering and data science skills in Gemini, Claude, and other large language models (LLMs). Teams can standardize on one set of component versions and move PySpark, Scala, and Spark SQL workloads between serverless and managed clusters.

Industry observers note that data teams should spend their time writing Spark logic rather than configuring infrastructure, hunting for the right job, or digging through driver and executor logs when something fails. Version 4.0 ships alongside a redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console built to take that operational work off their plate.

The refreshed console streamlines every stage of the Apache Spark lifecycle:.

Frictionless onboarding and one-click authoring: A redesigned Overview page helps developers get started immediately with an integrated samples gallery, pre-loaded Lakehouse public datasets, guided demos, and one-click authoring in VS Code through Cloud Shell.

It has been revealed that optimized defaults and reusable runtime profiles: Out-of-the-box performance defaults simplify job submission and cluster creation. With reusable runtime profiles (in preview) for batch and interactive workloads, platform admins can capture governed hardware, network, and autoscaling baselines once so developers can simply select a profile and run code.

Unified job, session, and fleet management: Engineers can submit and monitor batch jobs, interactive serverless sessions, and managed clusters from a single unified listing, backed by streamlined fleet management and redesigned detail views that surface key performance metrics and logs in one place.

Agentic troubleshooting: When a job fails or slows down, an AI agent analyzes logs, metrics, and query plans within existing IAM permissions to identify the likely root cause and recommend a fix, helping engineers quickly return a failed job to a healthy state.

Image 1: Gemini Cloud Assist investigates a failed Apache Spark job, forms a hypothesis, and points to the likely root cause without leaving the job page.

Image 2: One Jobs page for every Apache Spark workload across serverless and managed clusters, with tier and runtime version at a glance.

According to recent reports, many data engineers and data scientists would rather never leave their editor. With the Data Agent Kit, they can build and run Apache Spark workloads from VS Code, Antigravity, Claude Code, and other agentic IDEs. Setup takes a few clicks: pick Apache Spark and the other services you use, and the kit configures Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agent skills, and API access for each one. From there, AI agents can generate, tune, and test Apache Spark pipelines on Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 without leaving the IDE.

Image 3: In VS Code, the Data Agent Kit sets up MCP servers, skills, and API access for Apache Spark and other services.

Sources indicate that as practitioners and AI agents trigger short-running, ephemeral jobs on demand to prepare data, perform feature engineering, and answer ad-hoc queries, low startup latency and predictable price-performance are essential to avoiding a cost spiral. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, our performance-optimized serverless experience removes manual infrastructure tuning through three changes:.

Faster startups at no additional cost: On the serverless Premium tier, runtime and control-plane optimizations in version 4.0 deliver faster startup times than previous runtime versions across interactive sessions and short-running batch workloads at no additional cost.

Hardware acceleration by default: Fresh serverless 4.0 workloads run on the Premium tier by default, using Google Cloud's latest-generation Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk storage. Teams get our highest-efficiency compute and storage fleet without picking machine types or configuring disks, while aligning infrastructure tiering directly with workload urgency.

It has been revealed that software acceleration with Lightning Engine: Our native C++ vectorized execution engine, Lightning Engine, is available in the 4.0 runtime and delivers up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative, along with up to 4.9x faster performance compared to running open-source Apache Spark with zero code changes. Built on Apache Gluten and Velox with Google-specific optimizations, Lightning Engine compiles Apache Spark DataFrame, Dataset, and Spark SQL query intends into native SIMD instructions. For lakehouse storage, built-in intelligent caching accelerates file scan times on Apache Iceberg tables by up to 50%. Separately, for workloads querying BigQuery, Lightning Engine's native reader uses Apache Arrow streams to accelerate BigQuery reads by up to 40% compared to default BigQuery reads in Managed Service for Apache Spark. In the 4.0 runtime, Lightning Engine expands support to ARM processors, Ubuntu images, and native vectorized readers for Apache ORC and CSV alongside Apache Parquet, Apache Iceberg, and Delta Lake.

"We were facing not only processing challenges, we were facing management overhead across thousands of servers in our ecosystem, so we migrated to serverless Managed Service for Apache Spark. We moved from managing infrastructure to a no-ops infrastructure. Not only did it help us overcome maintenance and cluster management challenges, it helped us optimize our costs at scale to meet our business SLAs. Apache Spark is no longer just compute for us; it is a strategic business accelerator."—Saurabh Kumar, Senior Director of Data Engineering, Lowe's.

According to recent reports, when autonomous agents and production pipelines run around the clock, tying a workload to a single machine shape or zone can stall downstream decisions when regional demand spikes. Without dedicated reservations, cloud service providers may not always have available capacity during peak demand. We are introducing infrastructure fungibility for serverless deployments to improve resource availability for all customers:.

Recent findings suggest that serverless infrastructure fungibility and fallback: Serverless 4.0 workloads are no longer tied to one VM instance family, disk type, or zone. The platform selects from several latest-generation VM instance families and disk types across zones in the region. If the preferred infrastructure is constrained during a local demand peak, the service automatically chooses the best available infrastructure in the same region instead of failing the job. Once capacity returns, workloads go back to the default Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that data Compute Unit (DCU) quotas: Quotas for serverless deployments are now set in DCUs rather than per machine family. Because the platform selects the VM instance family, admins manage one unified DCU quota instead of separate CPU quotas for each machine type.

Industry observers note that A borderless lakehouse breaks down walled gardens by connecting operational, analytical, and cross-cloud data in open formats without moving it. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, Apache Iceberg ships directly in the runtime image, and every workload automatically has access to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. Teams no longer have to configure a lakehouse metastore with Apache Spark or complete prerequisites such as setting up Google Cloud Storage (GCS) directories beforehand, so they can focus straight on writing business logic. Version 4.0 also eliminates the need for GCS staging buckets and uses end-user credentials by default.

Recent findings suggest that through the Lakehouse runtime catalog, Managed Service for Apache Spark, BigQuery, and AlloyDB can directly read and write the same Apache Iceberg tables on GCS without ETL pipelines or data copies. Everything registered in the Lakehouse runtime catalog automatically surfaces in Knowledge Catalog, which enriches metadata and business context so AI agents and Gemini can query and reason over tables curated with Apache Spark with high accuracy, governed access controls, and lower token costs.

Recent findings suggest that to see how these capabilities come together across end-to-end architectures, read our Google Cloud Apache Spark in the Agentic Era whitepaper. The whitepaper walks through practical design patterns for multimodal data preparation, large-scale feature engineering, and connecting AI agents to governed Apache Iceberg tables through MCP tools and Knowledge Catalog.

According to recent reports, managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 is available for serverless and managed cluster deployments across all Managed Service for Apache Spark regions. The fastest way to try version 4.0 is the Data Agent Kit: install it in VS Code, Claude Code, or Antigravity to build and run Apache Spark workloads on version 4.0 with AI agents right from your IDE. You can also start from the new Overview page in the Google Cloud console, which walks you from code to a running job.

To learn more, read the Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 documentation for serverless deployments and managed clusters, and try the hands-on Lightning Engine codelab.

AWS Elemental MediaTailor adds Dynamic Avail Sizing for live HLS

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (205 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Elemental MediaTailor now supports Dynamic Avail Sizing, which reduces the slate viewers see when ad breaks, also called avails, in live HLS streams go unfilled.
  • When the ad decision server returns fewer ads than a break allows, dynamic avail sizing omits the unfilled time and resumes programming early instead of showing slate.
  • Customers turn on dynamic avail sizing for each playback session by adding query parameters to the session initialization URL, with no change to their playback configuration.

AWS Elemental MediaTailor now supports Dynamic Avail Sizing, which reduces the slate viewers see when ad breaks, also called avails, in live HLS streams go unfilled. MediaTailor is a server-side ad insertion and channel assembly service that personalizes ads in live and on-demand video streams.

When the ad decision server returns fewer ads than a break allows, dynamic avail sizing omits the unfilled time and resumes programming early instead of showing slate. To keep playback continuous, MediaTailor holds back a configurable reserve of content behind the live edge and draws on it when a break ends early. When the reserve runs low, MediaTailor requests extra ad time in later breaks to refill it. Free ad-supported streaming TV (FAST) channel operators can use dynamic avail sizing to keep viewers watching programming instead of filler content.

Customers turn on dynamic avail sizing for each playback session by adding query parameters to the session initialization URL, with no change to their playback configuration. To learn more, see Dynamic avail sizing in the AWS Elemental MediaTailor User Guide.

Dynamic avail sizing is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Elemental MediaTailor is available. For the full list of Regions, see the AWS Regional Services List.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In global maritime logistics, Marine Ports and Terminals play a significant role in the movement of container and cargo, within and beyond. Marine ports and terminals world-wide use a Terminal Operating System (TOS) which acts as the central nervous system managing port operations 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. A modern TOS intends, automates and orchestrates every physical and digital activities, resources and events across Order-to-Invoice processes of a marine terminal.

Developed by Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), DynaPORT is a field-proven next-generation Terminal Operating System that provides a single, integrated operating backbone for multimodal and multipurpose terminals. It orchestrates the complete order-to-invoice lifecycle across vessel, rail, truck, and barge operations, while supporting containers, general cargo, dry and liquid bulk, break-bulk, and roll-on/roll-off cargo. By automating end-to-end terminal workflows, DynaPORT delivers real-time operational visibility into operations while optimizing assets and resources to drive improvement of key business performance indicators.

It has been revealed that one of India’s largest commercial port developers and operators has relied on DynaPORT for more than two decades across its cargo terminals, supporting the management of bulk, break-bulk, and liquid cargo. To modernize the platform’s architecture, TCS partnered with the customer to achieve a landmark milestone: migrating DynaPORT to a modern, cloud-based architecture.

Sources indicate that the Port Operator & TCS partnered with Google Cloud to execute an ambitious cloud modernization journey. Modeled after the architectural principles of high-velocity Google Cloud enterprise transformations—this case study details the systematic deconstruction of legacy technical debt, the strategic rationale and enterprise differentiators of choosing AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, the target Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and AlloyDB cloud-native architecture, the heterogeneous migration of over 1.2 million lines of code using Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS).

According to recent reports, enterprise logistics platforms that evolve over decades inevitably accumulate architectural debt, particularly through tightly coupled components. DynaPORT Cargo followed this pattern: successive releases and architectural transitions gradually transformed the platform into a classic multi-tier monolith, with its components carrying significant technical debt.

Over years of optimization for sub-millisecond on-premises database round-trips, fundamental business logic had been progressively migrated out of the application tier and embedded directly into the database engine. In the DynaPORT Cargo module alone, the core schema contained:.

262 Packages containing over 1.2 million lines of code.

54 Stored Procedures, 53 Functions, and 63 Database Triggers.

Cross-schema User-Defined Types (UDTs).

Industry observers note that critical business operations—such as multi-tiered marine invoice tariff calculations, dynamic slab rating, berth allocation planning, yard truck assignments, and autonomous error logging—were entirely governed by complex, multi-thousand-line PL/SQL procedures. The database was no longer merely a relational persistence store; it was the primary execution engine of the enterprise.

The application tier was hosted on monolithic WebLogic and WildFly application servers running on static on-premises virtual machines. The application relied on legacy Java Enterprise features, including Enterprise JavaBeans (EJBs), custom Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) dialects, and heavy configuration state. Modules including Revenue Management, Berth Planning, Gate Operations, and Reporting shared common JVM heaps across application servers. A performance spike in batch invoice generation could starve memory from real-time Handheld Terminals (HHT) used by container crane operators on the quayside.

Because business logic was fragmented across Java application binaries and raw database packages, continuous delivery was practically non-existent:.

Manual Deployment Runbooks: Releases required multi-hour maintenance windows involving manual execution of sequential SQL scripts, package recompilations, and server restarts.

High Regression Risk: In the legacy schema with 262 interdependent packages, modifying a single package specification frequently invalidated dozens of dependent functions, views, and synonyms, triggering cascading runtime failures.

Environment Drift: Development, testing, and production environments suffered from configuration divergence, requiring lengthy manual reconciliation before any production cutover.

Licensing fees scaled linearly with physical CPU core counts, penalizing the business whenever hardware was scaled to accommodate peak cargo vessel traffic. Furthermore, high-availability setups required complex shared storage arrays, specialized interconnects, and heavy administrative overhead from dedicated database administrators (DBAs).

When architecting the cloud transformation, the joint architecture teams from the customer, TCS, and Google Cloud evaluated two fundamentally different modernization strategies:.

Strategy A: Database-Agnostic Migration.

Strategy B: Modernization using AlloyDB.

Extract all business logic from the database tier and rewrite it into Java application-tier services (HQL / Spring Data).

Retain optimized procedural logic in the database tier, converting to PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL on AlloyDB.

Massive. Complete rewrite of thousands of data access objects, ORM mappings, and transaction boundaries.

Recent findings suggest that moderate. Focused remediation of syntax, metadata, and database dialect differences; application remains stable.

Multiple person-years; prohibitive time-to-market.

Target delivery achievable in agile sprints; low operational disruption.

Network latency amplification due to multiple network hops for complex set operations previously run in-database.

Native in-engine execution with sub-millisecond response times, backed by AlloyDB’s accelerated storage and compute engine.

Rejected due to timeline risks and massive business disruption.

Selected as the winning enterprise target path.

The target cloud architecture was designed according to the Google Cloud Architecture Framework, transforming the monolithic JEE middleware into modern containerized microservices orchestrated on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), coupled with an enterprise AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster.

The cornerstone of the migration was converting over 1.2 million lines of deeply intertwined Oracle PL/SQL procedural logic into PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL. The team utilized Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS) with its built-in Conversion Workspaces and Gemini-assisted AI code refactoring to accelerate bulk transformations.

While DMS automatically converted the majority of standard DDL constructs, functions, and queries, the remaining (~15%) involved complex Oracle proprietary idioms that required targeted engineering remediation. Couple of examples of the manual intervention.

Technical Pattern & Remediation.

Modernized AlloyDB PL/pgSQL Equivalent.

Architectural Remediation & Runtime Impact.

TYPE_L := array_append(TYPE_L, rec); or TYPE_L[cardinality(TYPE_L)+1] := rec;.

Replaced unsupported .EXTEND method on nested tables with native PostgreSQL array concatenation and dynamic index expansion.

SELECT ROWNUM FROM PTY_IM WHERE ROWNUM <= N;.

SELECT s.idx FROM generate_series(1, N) AS s(idx);.

Eliminated physical dummy table hacks (PTY_IM) in favor of in-memory, set-returning generator functions with zero disk I/O.

Recent findings suggest that in April 2026, the modernized DynaPORT platform on Google Cloud went live in production at one of the newest ports in India, achieving a seamless, low downtime cutover. By Aug’26, 3 more terminals have gone live on this.

Modernized Google Cloud & AlloyDB Stack.

Variable query latency during batch spikes; table bloat requiring manual DBA reindexing.

Upto 2x transactional throughput, sub-second read query responses, automated ML vacuuming and memory optimization.

Complex SAN failover; multi-minute outages during planned database maintenance.

Sub-second automatic failover, 99.99% availability SLA inclusive of maintenance, zero transaction loss.

Multi-week release cycles; high-risk manual database patching; frequent regression challenges.

Containerized rolling updates on GKE and non-blocking transactional DDL deployments in AlloyDB.

Punitive per-core enterprise licenses; high on-prem hardware and maintenance overhead.

About 50% reduction in database TCO; completely open-source compatible with transparent, predictable cloud pricing.

Rigid vertical hardware limits; slow hardware procurement cycles.

Instantaneous horizontal elasticity across GKE container pods and AlloyDB read pools.

The successful cloud migration of DynaPORT yields three fundamental architectural lessons for enterprise IT leaders:.

It has been revealed that do Not Throw Away Proven Intellectual Property: Fully rewriting mission-critical procedural logic into application code is often a high-risk anti-pattern. Migrating from Oracle PL/SQL to open PL/pgSQL on an accelerated engine like AlloyDB preserves decades of tested business rules while modernizing the infrastructure platform.

Recent findings suggest that select Database Engines Built for Cloud Realities: Standard open-source relational engines often struggle with extreme enterprise throughput without extensive tuning. AlloyDB’s disaggregated storage architecture, columnar acceleration, and built-in ML intelligence provide the enterprise muscle needed to replace legacy commercial database engines.

Containerize Application Workloads on GKE: Decoupling the application tier into independently scalable container pods on Google Kubernetes Engine provides the elasticity and resilience necessary to absorb rapid operational surges without affecting core database stability.

Schedule a Google Cloud Architecture Blueprint Workshop with your Google Cloud Account Field team today. We will engage as an notable stakeholder to evaluate your current legacy setup and help design a low-risk, high-performance migration pathway using Google Cloud services like AlloyDB and Google Kubernetes Engine.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that.
  • And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

According to recent reports, GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so customers can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

According to recent reports, we suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

According to recent reports, no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

In a recent development, that is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

Industry observers note that for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

Recent findings suggest that the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

In a recent development, transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

It has been revealed that when GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

In a recent development, transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Recent findings suggest that our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

According to recent reports, A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

In a recent development, to show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Industry observers note that faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

It has been revealed that the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Sources indicate that transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

According to recent reports, these results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Recent findings suggest that performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve reveals the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

In a recent development, the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

According to recent reports, the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Sources indicate that the UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

In a recent development, once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

According to recent reports, reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

Latest Update: Welcome RL Environments to the hub

📅 28 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that reinforcement Learning environments give latest capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • In a recent development, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the newly introduced RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that reinforcement Learning environments give latest capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

In a recent development, an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the newly introduced RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, consumers of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a upcoming paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

In a recent development, the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Recent findings suggest that harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

It has been revealed that the viewer highlights the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

It has been revealed that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Industry observers note that here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

Sources indicate that the best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

AWS Transform now puts applications at the center of every stage of the migration journey, so you can discover, proposal, migrate, validate, and track the applications your business runs on rather than just the servers underneath them. Application-level grouping has been part of AWS rehost workflows for years, and AWS Transform now carries that same view through your entire migration.

According to recent reports, enterprise migrations typically involve thousands of servers, but the questions that drive decisions are about applications. Using discovery data, AWS Transform identifies application boundaries and dependencies, then surfaces logical groupings of applications, each with its own total cost of ownership (TCO) and migration tracking. AWS Transform also adds built-in surveys, letting application owners validate ownership, system boundaries, and business criticality.

A latest migration dashboard keeps everyone aligned as the migration moves forward. The dashboard pulls in data from every job in a workspace and updates as work progresses, so no one has to build or maintain separate status reports. You can customize the dashboard and ask questions about migration progress in chat.

This capability is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is offered. To learn more about migrating with AWS Transform, visit the product page.

How insured.io is transforming the customer experience for carriers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Founded in 2011, insured.io was created by a team that came from the California MGA market, where they saw first-hand how far the insurance customer experience lagged behind expectations, and where high levels of transient customers meant people were regularly interacting with insurance systems that often felt complicated, dated, and stale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Founded in 2011, insured.io was created by a team that came from the California MGA market, where they saw first-hand how far the insurance customer experience lagged behind expectations, and where high levels of transient customers meant people were regularly interacting with insurance systems that often felt complicated, dated, and stale.

In a recent development, according to Steve Johnson, Founder and Chief Product Officer at insured.io, that experience stayed with the founders as the tech giant evolved. After several years of building custom software for insurers, they decided in 2019 to launch a complete customer experience platform that carriers could deploy rapidly and easily configure around their needs.

For Johnson, the idea was straightforward – he wanted to give insurers a way to deliver a better customer experience without having to spend years designing and building it themselves, something that could be particularly valuable for mid-sized carriers that didn’t have the technical resources of the largest players.

It has been revealed that insured.io is a complete customer experience platform for insurance carriers. Johnson defines their raison d’etre simply; any digital channel, that a policyholder may need to interact with their insurance carrier, can be deployed as part of a single, integrated solution. This includes a policyholder portal, IVR, text messaging (both inbound and outbound), and conversational AI claims first notice of loss.

Industry observers note that johnson notes, “When a policyholder chooses a digital path to access their carrier online, it’s part of our platform. Our platform is designed to be scalable and configurable for any size of insurance carrier and any line of business, and our core tenet is future-proofing your customer experience, where customer expectations consistently outpace the technology that insurance carriers are able to implement.”.

He adds that insured.io has developed a platform that evolves over time, in order to continuously meet and exceed the expectations of policyholders without having to undergo constant waves of fresh digital transformations.

Recent findings suggest that being able to set yourself apart from others in the modern InsurTech industry is critical. For insured.io, the watchword here comes around being insurance-first.

Johnson explained, “I was an underwriter before I was in tech. Our entire executive team has come from the carrier side, so our platform is built with that mindset: we make technology that works for insurance, instead of making insurance work with our technology.”.

What the insured.io founder makes clear is that the manufacturer isn’t a ‘generic, repurposed, no-code platform’ that they decided could work for insurance.

“We’ve constructed everything from the ground-up specifically for this industry, and built for consistency across all channels,” he continued. “While your payment processor may give you a payment portal and a telecom vendor may handle your text messaging, we’re a truly omnichannel, vertical SaaS platform; through a singular integration with a policy management system, we can deploy all of these channels, so they’re all interconnected.”.

Additionally, the insured.io platform puts speed-to-market as a central plank, and Johnson believes this is something that has been lacking in the insurance market for a long time.

In a recent development, he remarked, “When it comes to implementing projects, especially with customer experience in mind, speed-tomarket is paramount because you don’t want to get caught in an infinite development process, where by the time you launch, whatever you’ve done is now out of date. Our goal is to always get introduced within 90 days.”.

A stumbling block for some firms in the InsurTech market has been mistaking digitisation for better CX.

In the view of Johnson, digitisation is a piece of the puzzle, but it isn’t the whole package.

“Customer experience is truly its own discipline, and it has its own unique solutions outside of the scope of just digitisation ,’ he mentioned. “The sole act of digital transformation is not necessarily solving for CX. While solving insurance inefficiency can lead to better CX, you must take a targeted approach when it comes to today’s policyholders.”.

Johnson believes that on this matter, it takes a focus on CX to improve it, and it’s not just a side effect of improving components within the insurance ecosystem.

A key question posed to Johnson is whether insurers are optimising for efficiency at the expense of experience. Does he believe this?

Sources indicate that “I think this is true, but it’s not necessarily on purpose,” he stated. “It comes from a lack of understanding about what a good user experience for policyholders is. What may be the most efficient internally isn’t necessarily the solution to keep your policyholders satisfied.

Recent findings suggest that “Implementing a chatbot, for example, can be a great example of embracing technology at the expense of the user experience.” said Johnson. “A chatbot should not just be a feather in your technological cap, it must solve real problems for real customers. Otherwise, your fresh efficiency might inadvertently cost you customers and time.”.

All of these things combined together, Johnson remarks, show how key it is to target customer experience the right way.

On the question of whether claims experience is still the defining chapter in the insurance CX, Johnson is succinct, “You don’t get your Yelp reviews from the quality of your underwriting or your actuarial skills. They come from how good or bad the claims process is.”.

Industry observers note that johnson added that insurers are much less likely to get a positive review for a good claims experience than they are to get a negative review for a poor one. This, he states, means focusing on improving the claims experience is a huge piece of the puzzle.

He remarked, “One thing that is crucial for this is realtime claim status. Some 30% of calls coming into a claims department are just to see what is going on with their claim, and that’s because many insurance carriers lack the key piece of the claims puzzle, which is claim status tracking – what we call the pizza tracker of claims.”.

Recent findings suggest that when you’re able to see where your pizza is from the moment it goes in the oven to the moment it arrives at your doorstep, insurance has no excuse. Claimants often have no idea what an adjuster is doing at any given time, which causes frustration and increases call volume.

A key question facing the InsurTech industry right now is what happens when customer expectations outpace insurance infrastructure.

Johnson believes this has been a problem since the time the ‘very first insurance policy was ever written’.

He explains, “Customer expectations will always outpace insurance infrastructure. Insurance has been notoriously slow to adopt upcoming technologies than other verticals. It’s a regulated industry, so it’s certainly easier to implement new technology when you’re selling pizzas than when you’re selling insurance policies.”.

Johnson states his belief that this will always cause challenges internally. Such complications, he believes, come up around build vs buy, vendor sprawl, and the need to constantly play catch up with customer expectations. All of these issues run alongside the crucial need of still providing high-quality insurance products.

In a recent development, johnson concluded, “One of the mistakes that is often made is insurance executives trying to design customer experience. It’s never a good idea to design these things by committee, because a focus is on loss ratios, reducing claims, and making sure you collect as much premium as possible may not always align with building a great customer experience. Ultimately, this is why it’s all about finding the right customer facing solutions that can effectively marry all of these concepts together, making the insurance process painless for the consumer from end-to-end.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that holo4 is our new series of agentic models.
  • It has been revealed that holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • In a recent development, holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

It has been revealed that holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

In a recent development, holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Recent findings suggest that holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

In a recent development, holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

In a recent development, trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

In a recent development, the tower is square in strategy at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Holo4 27B (84 calls, 1.3M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (60 calls, 1.0M tokens).

In a recent development, build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H firm logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Holo4 27B (94 calls, 1.5M tokens).

Qwen3.8 27B (118 calls, 1.9M tokens).

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

In a recent development, our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Industry observers note that alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Recent findings suggest that our post-training stack is designed to adapt to upcoming foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Recent findings suggest that both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#18542. Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1648 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse.
  • In a recent development, other disciplines test differently.
  • Industry observers note that data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Software Engineer, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

Technical Lead, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse. Ideally, you'd develop and test it against production data, but access restrictions and data sensitivity make that difficult – especially when the engineers building the agent sit outside the team that owns the data. Even with access, a live warehouse is a poor test track: Catalog descriptions are often incomplete or contradicted by institutional knowledge in docs and chat threads; there’s no verified answer key across its thousands of tables; and you can't systematically vary the complexity of the data and documents to see where the agent breaks. So teams often test on toy datasets and hope the agent holds up in production.

In a recent development, other disciplines test differently. Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges. A shape that performs well in the tunnel performs well on the road because the tunnel preserves the physical properties the shape responds to.

Industry observers note that data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a company's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document. It is designed to preserve what the agent reasons over: how tables relate, what business events create which records, where institutional knowledge lives, and how definitions get messy. When those properties hold, an agent's behavior in the tunnel tracks its behavior on production data, even though the two share no sensitive content.

At Google, we built an internal data simulator to serve as a wind tunnel for our enterprise data agents. Rather than copying proprietary schemas or cataloging every undocumented quirk in a live warehouse, an engineer starts with a short, plain-English description of organizational patterns, for example: "Simulate a two-plant brake manufacturer with an ERP, a shop-floor execution system, and a three-shift schedule where second-shift supervisors track downtime differently from operations and finance." From just a few sentences, the simulator invents a structurally analogous company ("Calder Brakes"), generating its schemas, rows, event history, documents, and chat threads alongside a benchmark of hard questions and a verified answer key.

Figure 1. Production data and its synthetic counterpart share causal structure without sharing sensitive content. A short description of domain patterns seeds the wind tunnel, where the agent is evaluated over read-only tools and behavioral trends carry back to production.

Why did we do this? Most data agents are evaluated on small, clean test databases with well-labeled tables, unambiguous metrics, and no conflicting documents. Those datasets are convenient, but they rarely test the judgment that enterprise data demands.

Once generated, a synthetic estate is served through a read-only interface — SQL execution, schema browsing, and document search — that any agent can call without seeing the blueprint or answer key. But consider what happens when an agent is asked either a qualitative onboarding question or a quantitative metric question from our simulated factory, "Calder Brakes Plant 2":.

Recent findings suggest that qualitative: "A fresh analyst is joining the team. What should they know about how 'downtime' is handled here, before they start producing reports?".

Recent findings suggest that A naive agent falls into the same trap on both questions. It searches for the most authoritative document and finds a policy memo from Bob, a second-shift supervisor, which states that downtime means unplanned stoppages only, and planned changeovers don't count. Bob is confident, articulate, and senior, so the agent summarizes his definition — and filters out planned changeovers when writing its SQL query.

Industry observers note that both answers are wrong. In fact, the plant's official metric counts changeovers as planned downtime. Bob sincerely believes his version because it flatters his shift's numbers, but weeks later the metric owner quietly corrects the record in a follow-up thread. Getting either question right requires looking past a document's tone, checking who owns the metric before writing SQL, and tracing later corrections. This is where data agents often fail in production.

In a recent development, A synthetic estate is only useful for evaluation if its answer key is accurate and reproducible. Our simulator achieves this by separating simulated organization’s design from data generation across four stages (Figure 2).

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. One pipeline, one source of truth. In the estate-generation pipeline, only ① Compile blueprint invents facts and ③ Render documents phrases those fixed facts as prose (blue boxes); ② Simulate & build tables (plus SQL answer computation) runs deterministically from the frozen blueprint and seed, before ④ Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

First, the Compile blueprint stage uses a language model to turn the pattern prompt into a frozen blueprint specifying the company's systems, people, metrics, and individual beliefs. Those beliefs can be mistaken on purpose — Bob's flawed definition of downtime is recorded alongside the official metric, planting the trap and its solution together.

In the estate-generation pipeline, Compile blueprint is the only point where a language model decides what is true. Once the blueprint is frozen, Simulate & build tables runs deterministically without a model: employees act on their schedules, triggering tickets, shift handovers, and database rows, so that every record traces back to the event that created it. Organizational messiness emerges naturally from this timeline, such as outdated procedures or conflicting definitions, while row-level flaws that model real ingestion glitches (e.g., retry-storm duplicate rows, unmerged keys, or a mid-quarter unit change) are injected into the tables. Every flaw is recorded in a machine-readable messiness log so the benchmark generator can adjust the ground-truth SQL queries to account for the messy tables.

According to recent reports, given the same blueprint and random seed, the simulator produces identical tables and an identical SQL answer key on every run. The only subsequent step in building the estate that calls a model is Render documents, which turns the facts fixed in the blueprint into memos and chat threads in each person's writing style. Finally, Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

Three build-time checks keep the benchmark honest:.

Computed SQL and rubric gold answers: Every quantitative question ships with the SQL query that computes its expected ("gold") answer against the messy tables. Because the messiness log records injected retry duplicates on defect rows, the benchmark generator automatically pairs a defect-count question with the deduplicating COUNT(DISTINCT) query (240) – and runs decoy SQL queries representing common mistakes (like an un-deduplicated COUNT(*) or Bob's changeover filter) to verify that falling for a trap yields a different number. Qualitative questions ship with a rubric grounded in the blueprint's metric owner, official definition, and correction trail. If the estate lacks the data to verify a question, the generator drops the item rather than shipping an unverified question.

Verified documents: Every rendered memo and chat thread is checked against the blueprint to confirm it states its assigned facts without introducing unrecorded numbers, dates, or names.

Hallucination sentinels: The simulator plants questions about invented metrics like "Basalt Velocity Ratio" that appear nowhere in the estate; a reliable agent abstains and reports that no such metric exists.

A wind tunnel does not need to match the exact score an agent gets on production data; it needs to reproduce the same behavioral trends: direction (if longer reasoning chains lower accuracy on real data, they should lower accuracy in the tunnel) and rate (accuracy should degrade at the similar pace as contradictions accumulate). When those trends hold, you can confidently compare agent versions and dial up complexity step by step to find where reasoning breaks down.

We test how closely our simulated estates match reality — and whether evaluation signals carry over — at three levels:.

According to recent reports, our simulator builds on two research threads. In database question answering, benchmarks like BIRD and Spider 2.0 have moved from clean schemas to messy databases, while agent environments like WebArena, tool-use benchmarks like τ-bench, and Generative Agents simulate websites or use language models to role-play human customers. In contrast, our simulator's employees follow deterministic rules tied to their roles and schedules, so a single seed replays the exact same organizational history every time.

Sources indicate that we also adapt an intuition from domain randomization in robotics, where simulations vary surface details like lighting and textures during training while keeping the underlying physics faithful. Applied to data agent evaluation, that means synthesizing every surface name, number, and document from a short pattern description, while keeping the causal structure, cross-document links, and institutional messiness faithful to enterprise reality.

Recent findings suggest that generating a test estate on demand removes a bottleneck between enterprises that own sensitive data, and the engineering teams building data agents for them. Traditionally, developing and benchmarking an enterprise agent required access to production tables and a hand-labeled question set — the two assets hardest to share across organizational or compliance boundaries. We use this wind tunnel internally to stress-test and harden Google Cloud's data agents against realistic enterprise messiness without touching customer data, and the same blueprint-first architecture can be applied by any engineering team building evaluation suites for their own agents.

Synthetic evaluation still carries two risks: overfitting to the simulator's patterns of messiness, and drift as a live business evolves away from its blueprint. The discipline required is the same one that wind-tunnel engineers practice: Periodically calibrate the tunnel against real-world runs, keep benchmark difficulty aligned with production failure modes, and treat the simulation as a living model. Your agents — and their consumers — will thank you.

Sources indicate that AWS Transform for migrations now combines migration assessment and migration planning into a single migration job. Previously, you ran separate jobs to build a total cost of ownership (TCO) business case and to plan your migration. With this launch, you upload your on-premises inventory once and use it for both assessment and planning, in any order.

After you upload your inventory data, you can estimate your AWS costs and build a business case, group your infrastructure into applications and plan migration waves, or do both. You can rerun either workflow as your data improves. For example, build a business case first and then plan waves from the same inventory, or plan your waves first and then estimate the cost of a single wave. Because assessment and planning share one inventory, your business case and migration plan stay consistent without moving data between jobs. After you finalize your plan and assessment, you can continue in the same job to migrate your networks, deploy landing zones, and migrate servers, storage, and containers.

According to recent reports, this newest release is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Transform is offered. To learn more about migrating with AWS Transform, visit the product page and documentation.

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1819 w)
